en: Spandakārikā,
the first natural outflow:
He whose opening and closing of the eyes constitute the dissolution and emergence of the universe.
We praise that Śaṅkara, the source of the manifestation of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*).

We praise this Śaṅkara, our own true nature, who bestows grace—the very essence of which is the recognition of the expansion of one’s own consciousness as non-dual supreme bliss, wherein all afflictions have been completely stilled; we praise him while perceiving him as transcending the entire universe.

We enter by means of immersing ourselves in the state of the subject as fashioned and conceptualized therein; for it is this very immersion that is taught in this treatise as the fruit of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). The use of the plural number is intended to manifest the non-difference of all those to be graced, who are looked upon with a glance of grace.
By the word "that" (*tam*), that which was also implied by its uniqueness is now made explicit by the half-verse beginning with "of whom" (*yasya*).

Here, the Supreme Lord, Mahādeva, whose essence is Light, is by nature the full sovereignty consisting of the two-fold creative emission (*visarga*)— the friction-sticks (*araṇi*) for which are the supreme power (*parāśakti*) and the nature of the dense vibration of bliss— which arises from being the core of the reflective awareness of the Great "I" (*mahāhaṃtā*), the ultimate reality of the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*).

Precisely because of that very nature of consciousness, although the venerable Lord is immovable, His power of absolute freedom—though undivided from Him—manifests the entire succession of emanation, withdrawal, and so forth, upon its own ground like a city in a mirror; by means of a future logic, it appears as if augmented though not actually increased.

Because it conforms to the meaning of verbal roots characterized by slight movement, it is designated as *spanda* (vibration). Therefore, the Lord is eternally of the same essence as the reality of *spanda*.
But it is not motionless, as some have said that the supreme reality is motionless (*aspanda*).

For if it were so, because its essential nature would be quiescent, it would be devoid of sovereignty (*anīśvara*). Indeed, this scripture titled *Samucita-spanda* was composed by the Great Teachers precisely to demonstrate one's own true nature as Śaṅkara, which consists of the power of vibration whose essence is radiant pulsation (*sphurattā*).
And this will become clear [later].

This very power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*), which consists of the bliss of the wonder of the "I-consciousness" (*ahantā*)—a single mass in which infinite emanations and withdrawals are internalized;

whose true nature is the manifestation of the contraction and expansion of all subjects and objects, whether entirely pure or impure; and which is to be meditated upon by all the Upaniṣads, exists simultaneously.
Thus, she consists of both opening (unmeṣa) and closing (nimeṣa).

For indeed, that which is the state of closing (nimeṣabhū), consisting of the form of the destroyer of the entire aggregate of principles (tattva) beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth that was previously created, is itself the ground of opening (unmeṣabhūmi) consisting of the form of the creator with respect to the state yet to arise; likewise, it is the ground of the closing of the universe.

The essence of the unfolding of the density of consciousness (*cidghana*) is also the ground of immersion into that same density of consciousness, yet it takes the form of the universal unfolding (*viśvonmeṣa*).
As the scripture says:
"The Goddess, ever-licking and ever-full, shines eternally. (VSpkC 1.1:10)
"This wave of the ocean of consciousness is the power of the Lord, whose nature is will. Thus [it is said].

For the illustrious Maheśvara, by means of his power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*), [projects] from Śiva down to the Mantra-Maheśvaras, the Mantreśvaras, the Mantras, the Vijñānākala, the Pralayākala, and the Sakala.

Assuming the stage of the subject (*pramātṛ*) and the stage of its object (*vedya*), while causing the preceding preceding forms— which stand as the foundational wall— to close their eyes through the play of concealing His own inner nature, He causes them to open [to the next]; and by means of the process of descent,
He causes the subsequent forms to close their eyes, while by the process of ascent, He causes the knowledge-yogis to open their eyes to each successive preceding form.
For this very reason, each subsequent [level] causes that which precedes it to abandon its nature of contraction by manifesting it as expansion;
conversely, each preceding form causes the subsequent expansion to submerge and presents itself as contracted.

And thus, He manifests everything as being composed of everything; it is only due to the mere contraction manifested therein that there appears to be this perception of difference, for which purpose the instruction is given here to uproot it—let this suffice.
This much for now.

Furthermore, consciousness—which consists of the unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of appearances such as blue, pleasure, and so forth—is also characterized by the closing (*nimeṣa*) of its own nature, which is the single essence of the subject; it takes the form of withdrawing appearances such as yellow that have already been manifested.
Thus, one should recognize this divine intuition (*pratibhā*), established through self-awareness, as having the dual form of both unfolding and closing simultaneously.

The great-minded ones, however, investigate [this] for the sake of severing the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*). For this very reason, in his own commentary (*nijavṛtti*), the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa explained the phrase "by means of opening and closing" (*unmeṣanimeṣābhyām*) as being inseparable from "by mere volition" (*saṃkalpamātreṇa*), insofar as it consists of the power of will (*icchāśakti*). The author of the compendium (*saṃgrahakṛt*) also stated: "Because for one who is intent upon a single thought, there arises the emergence of another."

"That, however, should be known as *unmeṣa* (the unfolding); one should personally discern it. Regarding this, it will be stated that the very withdrawal of commenced thought is the cause for the arising of the supreme nature (*parasvarūpa*), because without the withdrawal of active thought, there is no arising of the supreme nature. And we shall elaborate upon this in that very place.
"The depletion of the supreme nectar for him is that which arises from conditions;
by that, he attains a state of non-sovereignty, and that [depletion] has as its object only those [conditions].
Thus, even here, it will be clearly stated that arising is the ultimate reality of dissolution.

"When agitation (*kṣobha*) dissolves, then the supreme state (*paramaṃ padam*) arises. (VSpkC 1.1:24) Here too, it will be demonstrated that the momentary closing (*nimeṣa*), which consists of the dissolution of agitation, is itself the nature of the opening (*unmeṣa*) of the supreme state. (VSpkC 1.1:25) Thus, although power (*śakti*) is one and possesses both forms, it is sometimes designated as being primarily characterized by opening (*unmeṣa*), and sometimes as being primarily characterized by closing (*nimeṣa*). (VSpkC 1.1:26)

And thus, from that [Supreme Cause], by means of the power (*śakti*) belonging to it— which consists in the unfolding of its own nature (*svarūponmeṣa*), is primarily characterized by the manifestation of effects, and is the cause of the emergence of the entire universe from Śiva down to the earth— a creation (*sarga*) arises that possesses manifold variety and takes the form of differentiation (*bheda*), yet whose essence is the submergence in non-difference (*abheda*). Furthermore, by means of the power which consists in the closing of its own nature (*svarūponmeṣa*) and is primarily characterized by the closing toward externality (*bāhyatānimeṣa*), there occurs the dissolution (*pralaya*) of the universe.

"One whose nature is the arising consisting of differentiation is the withdrawal of the state of manifold differentiated forms; thus, even dissolution has the form of arising, and even arising has the form of dissolution—this is how it should be explained. In reality, however, nothing at all arises or perishes; rather, it is only the Blessed One’s power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*), though itself beyond succession, which, throbbing as the form of various such manifestations, seems to arise and seems to perish."
We shall demonstrate this.

Since maintenance, dissolution, and grace consist essentially of specific forms of dissolution and emergence, there is no addition [to the categories]; thus, the fivefold sovereign activity (*pārameśvaryakṛtya*) is subsumed within dissolution and emergence alone. Furthermore, such a point has been determined by me myself in the *Spandasandoha*, which is a commentary on the first sūtra alone.

Now, one might object: "If the diverse dissolution and emergence of the world are accomplished by the deities of emission and so forth alone through the vision of the glorious Great Purpose (*mahārtha*), then how can it be said [in the verse], 'of whom' and so on? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "He who is the source of the manifestation of the power-circle" (*taṃ śakticakravibhavaprabhavam*).

The "circle of powers" (*śakticakra*) refers to the twelvefold assembly of the goddesses of rays, such as Sṛṣṭi, Rakta, and the rest. Its "manifestation" (*vibhava*) consists of its playful display (*krīḍāḍambara*), which has the nature of exertion (*udyoga*), illumination (*avabhāsana*), consumption (*carvaṇa*), and dissolution (*vilāpana*); he is the "source" (*prabhava*) of that.
The cause.

For this is the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*): these goddesses, having embraced the glorious Manthānabhairava, the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśvara*), accomplish the play of the creation and so forth of the entire universe at all times.

Now, as to the doubt—why does the Supreme Lord possess the status of being the cause of the creation, destruction, and so forth of the universe?—the answer to this is precisely "the wheel of powers" (*śakticakra*).

For whatever in the universe comes into being does so by virtue of its being manifest, because it consists of light; and thus, the manifestation of the multitude of entities residing within the Self belongs to the Lord. (VSpkC 1.1:34) "Therefore, the reflective awareness of will (*icchāmarśa*) proceeds only when [the Lord] exists. (VSpkC 1.1:35) According to this principle established by the wise, that which exists as manifest through identity with the internal light of the Supreme Lord is called the "wheel of powers" (*śakticakra*). This is because the Supreme Lord is described in the scriptures as possessing infinite powers.
It is proclaimed:

the source, that is, the cause, of the manifestation—that is, the infinite variety of conjunctions and disjunctions—of that universe which consists of the supreme reality appearing as the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*).

For that very Lord, by joining and separating all appearances—which consist of the body of consciousness and abide in identity with His own Self—in their mutual manifold variety, is the cause of the emergence and dissolution of the universe.

Thus it was stated by the venerable Bhaṭṭakallaṭa regarding the Lord’s sovereignty over the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), which consists of the body of consciousness, being the cause of its manifestation.
(VSpkC 1.1:39) Thus, the correspondence between these words of the commentary and both of these two interpretations is established. (VSpkC 1.1:40)

Moreover, "His powers are the entire universe"—according to the perspective of the scriptures (*āgama*). And according to the principle established here: "Therefore, in the contemplation of word and meaning, there is no state that is not Śiva.
Thus, for one whose self is the universe, [the reality] is the sky situated on the upward path of the Sky-farer (*khecarī*), which is the domain of Vāmeśī.

Thus, according to the secret principle, [it has been stated] by me alone in the *Spandasandoha* that those whose forms are Vāmeśvarī, Khecarī, Gocarī, Dikcarī, and Bhūcarī are intent on concealing their own state for those of unawakened intellect; and this will also be determined here as being the manifestation of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) explained in these two commentaries. Since this group of instruments (the senses) exists in such a state—as expressed in the verse:
"Having seized the power of this collection of senses" (VSpkC 1.1:46)—[the mantras act].
Thus, according to this principle, regarding the majesty (*vibhava*)—

that is, the greatness (*māhātmya*)— of the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), which consists of the nature of deities such as Brāhmī and so forth, which arises from the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*) that are the essence of the eternal mantra, and which is of infinite varieties beginning with these [deities], and which has been extensively determined by me alone in the *Spandasandoha* as being "the source" (*prabhava*) because it prevails therein; [this is the meaning].
It is independent, not dependent like a bound soul (*paśu*).

By means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound— referring to that whose origin, emergence, and manifestation proceed from the power (*vibhava*) of the wheel of energies (*śakticakra*), which is a mass of rays, and whose expansion is inward-turned— the recognition of the nature of the Supreme Lord occurs effortlessly through the contemplation of that inward-turned essential nature.
This is the meaning: "it comes into being.

Furthermore, through the opening and closing—the manifestation and withdrawal—of that Self which is a mass of consciousness and bliss, by the logic that "what is within is without," there arises [the world] of the universe, both the body-form of the world and the external world associated with it.

We praise Śaṅkara, the source of the manifestation of the power-circle (śakticakra) and the expansion of the deity of supreme consciousness (parasaṃvid), who reveals this true nature to those possessed of devotion; for him, dissolution and emergence occur respectively as submergence and surfacing.
Likewise, from the unfolding (unmeṣa) of his own self—which consists of the outward-turning flow—there arises the emergence of the world.

And because of the closing (*nimeṣa*) which consists of inward-turnedness, there is dissolution; we praise Śaṅkara, the cause of that [dissolution] and of the majesty of the Goddess of Consciousness whose nature consists of the unfolding (*unmeṣa*) of the effects such as the creation of the universe—this may also be applied according to the context. (VSpkC 1.1:51) Even though the Supreme Lord is entered into the body and so forth, by means of the opening and closing of the instruments (*karaṇa*), He performs the creation and withdrawal of the world consisting of the fivefold objects such as form. (VSpkC 1.1:52)

As it has been stated by the knower of the secret reality: "In this way, even in the sphere of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), the Lord, entering the body and so forth, may manifest externally by his own will the very flood of objects that was already shining within. Thus, for the sake of grasping such objects, the Guru described [the Lord] as having "sovereign power" (*svātantrya-śakti*)—abandoning the phrasing "by whose opening and closing [of the eyes]"—as one who acts through that sovereign power. (VSpkC 1.1:53–55)

And here, the praise of Śaṅkara—which consists of immersion—is the subject matter to be attained. By means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, "that from which there is manifestation (*prabhava*) due to the power of the wheel of energies (*śakticakra-vibhava*)," the expansion of the wheel of energies is stated to be the means for attaining that [subject].

By means of a *tatpuruṣa* compound, "the manifestation (*prakāśaka*) of the power of the wheel of energies—the expansion of the deity of supreme consciousness—for those possessing devotion," the fruit is stated.
It has been stated:

"That which he will say [is that] 'thereafter one becomes the Lord of the Wheel' (cakreśvara). Thus, the relationship between the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the means (*upāya*)—namely, the state of being the goal (*upeya*) and the means (*upāya*)—as well as the purpose (*prayojana*), have all been indicated by this very aphorism.
Now, what is the proof for the existence of Śaṅkara’s nature in such a state? Furthermore, from what material cause (*upādāna*) does he produce the world without a cause?

If he himself were the material cause, then the world would obscure him, just as a jar obscures a lump of clay; and if there were a state of being both obscured and unobscured, there would be a difference in the Lord's own nature. Moreover, a cause for his re-emergence must be considered, and in the arising of the world, there would be the undesirable consequence of duality.
To remove these doubts with a single stroke, he says:
"Wherein all this effect is situated and from which it has emerged—because its nature is unobstructed, there is no cessation anywhere. (VSpk 1.2)

For this very Śiva-nature, which is a mass of light and bliss and is one's own essential being (*svasvabhāva*), there is no obstruction—no restriction on its expansion—in any place, time, or form, because its nature is unobscured and its essence is never covered. This is the meaning: whatever here might be conceived as an obscuration of the light of consciousness (citprakāśa)—be it the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), pleasure, or the color blue—if that does not shine forth, it is nothing at all; but that which does shine forth is indeed the very nature of Śiva, whose essence is light. What [else could it be]?
Of what is it the destroyer, or what is the meaning of its cessation?
This very point—that "it belongs to that"—is established by the qualification beginning with "wherein," and so forth.
Wherein, in which form within itself, this entire world-effect consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge is situated.

How could that which, being manifest through the light of another, attains its stability, be suppressed by that very [light]? For if it were suppressed, that which is intended as the suppressor itself would not shine forth; this is the underlying intention.
As it has been said:
"How could there be for him any constraint by means of the vital breath (prāṇa) through that very self?"—thus [it is said] in the *Ajadapramātṛsiddhi*.

Now, one might ask: "Granted that for that which has arisen, its nature is stability within manifestation; but from where does its very arising come? To this he says: "And because it has emerged from... (VSpkC_1.2:7).

Having set aside the causality of the world as established by the consciousness’s own experience—viewed through the lens of memory, dreams, mental constructs, and the emanations of yogis—it is not reasonable to postulate [causality] for the *pradhāna*, atoms, and so forth, which are neither supported by valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇaka*) nor logically tenable (*anupapanna*). This very point is implied by the word "effect" (*kārya*); for an effect is defined as that which is produced by the action of an agent, and not something that merely follows upon an insentient cause, since the causality of an insentient entity is untenable, according to the principle stated in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.
And this will come to pass:
"In this context, there are two states designated as 'the state of being an agent' and 'the state of being an effect.
(VSpkC 1.2:10–11) Thus [it is said] here.
By the word "all" (*sarva*), it is implied that the agent is independent of material causes (*upādāna*) and so forth.
Furthermore, an effect such as a jar is never observed to conceal the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of its maker, such as a potter.

[Objection: But surely emergence occurs for that which was already present; therefore, does this [effect] exist from the very beginning? [Reply: It is not situated elsewhere, but rather in that very Self of Consciousness (*cidātman*). To this he says: "wherein it is situated. (VSpkC 1.2:14)
And this should be applied by way of reversal (*āvṛttyā*).

This is the meaning: if the world did not exist within the conscious Self (*cidātman*) as non-different from the manifestation of "I," how could it arise from that [Self] independently of material causes and so forth?
For, just as a great tree exists in the form of a potentiality within the seed of a *nyagrodha* tree...
"Thus, this entire world, both moving and non-moving, resides within the seed-syllable of the heart"—
according to the established tradition of the scriptures;
[and] "of the Lord who abides within the self."

Thus, by the reasoning previously stated, it remains there shining forth non-differently; therefore, it is logical that this Lord, whose nature is consciousness (*cidātman*), causes the world—which consists of the solidification of His own essence—to emerge.

(VSpkC 1.2:20) And thus, the connection is established here: "that from which [the world] has emerged while remaining [identical with Him]. (VSpkC 1.2:21) The particle *ca* is used in the sense of "and" (*eva-arthe*), though its position in the sequence is displaced. (VSpkC 1.2:22)

Now, one might object: "If this world has emerged from that whose nature is light (*prakāśavapus*), then it would not be manifest; for it is illogical that something external to manifestation should yet be manifested.
Anticipating this doubt, the connection [of the verse] should be understood through repetition as follows: "Even though it has emerged from that, it remains situated therein. (VSpkC 1.2:23)
The word "even" (*api*) has been displaced in the sequence [of the verse].

This is what is meant: it is not that the walnuts and so forth have emerged from a bag or similar container; rather, it is that very Blessed One who, through his own sovereignty, displays upon his own screen the form of the world—as if it were something distinct, though not actually distinct—like a city in a mirror.
...remaining while manifesting [it].

Now, one might object: "Granted that the world remains unobstructed during the states of creation and maintenance, how is it not concealed by the state of dissolution—which is of the nature of non-existence and resembles deep sleep—since [the world] is connected to that [state]? For it is not [the case that it is not concealed].

The meaning is this: by repeating the statement that "the object of apprehension is the world, while the subject of apprehension is the conscious self (cidātman)," this very same [consciousness] is the answer.
For even though the world has emerged from it, and even though it has arisen, it remains in the state of dissolution as being of one essence with that very [consciousness];

there is no other destruction of it in the form of a void, because—as will be explained by the reasoning to follow—it is impossible for anything to exist without consciousness, which serves as its foundational wall.
As it is said in the Śrī Svacchandaśāstra:

"It is said that the non-empty is emptiness, and emptiness is called non-existence. That non-existence, O Goddess, should be known as that wherein all existents have gone to their destruction. (VSpkC 1.2:27)
Thus:

"In this way, for that whose every effect is manifested only by its own manifestation, and which, even when withdrawn, remains as one with that very manifestation—for such a one, no factor such as space, time, or form can logically serve as a restrictor; therefore, it is all-pervading, eternal, and inlaid with the powers of the universe."

This reality is self-luminous and established from the beginning; therefore, for its establishment, there is no need for, nor is it possible for, the wretched instrument of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—which consists in the illumination of an unknown object—to arise or be applicable.
On the contrary, the establishment of the entire universe, including the instruments of valid cognition and so forth, is dependent upon the establishment of this very reality.
As it was said by our teachers in the *Tantrāloka*:
"Even those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which extend the life of entities—
their supreme life-force is that very same Supreme Lord. Thus [it is said].

For even this world, though it has emerged from that [Reality], remains situated within it; though it appears by means of its light, it remains as it truly is, situated within that which is of the singular nature of light and is that very light itself. It is for the sake of the realization of that [light] alone that everything is perceived in its entirety, and not because there exists any other thing called "the world."
* Here, the phrase "where it is situated" (*yatra sthitam*) should be repeated and applied twice.

* Thus, the perpetual and omnipresent non-obstruction of this reality—which manifests as creation, maintenance, withdrawal, and their integration, and which performs what is otherwise most difficult to accomplish—is established by one's own direct experience.
As it was stated by the venerable teacher Utpaladeva:
"Victorious is Your unprecedented state of supreme lordship, O Lord of All, which is devoid of anything to be ruled;
and likewise victorious is Your other [state], by which this world appears in such a way that it does not truly appear.
* Here, the meaning is that the world, while appearing, is nothing other than appearance itself; because appearance is its sole remainder, nothing appears apart from appearance.

Furthermore, by the expression "wherein it is situated," there is the state of cessation (*upaśama-pada*); and by the expression "from whence it has emerged," there is the state of expansion (*prasara-pada*).

Since there is no cessation of this [world] therein, the yogin, intent on immersion into his own true nature (*svabhāva-samāveśa*), should remain so even in both the two types of samādhi: closing and opening.
It must be so.
As it will be said:
"When agitation has dissolved, then there shall be the supreme state."
Thus it is said:
"Therefore, among all reflections upon words and their meanings, there is no state that is not auspicious."
And furthermore: Even when there exists some cognizer, such as a follower of the Sugata who propounds non-self, and some means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that is considered subverting,
there is no cessation— that is, no negation— of that [cognizer], because both the one who would negate it and the means by which it would be negated [are themselves subject to the same critique].

If that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not established, then this [argument] is like a painting without a wall; yet its establishment is manifest. Therefore, by the very establishment of that [means], it is stated—though in words that deny it—that the Blessed One exists as one whose form is primordially established self-luminosity (*svaprakāśamūrti*). This will also be explained later.
"But not that state which is introverted"—
in this interval [it is said]: "And thus, by this [means],

one realizes the nature of Śiva, which transcends the universe, yet consists of the universe, and performs the creation, dissolution, and so forth of the universe, being the very essence of one's own true nature."
By the one who declares "this is the reality" (*tattva*), that which is to be worshipped in all the scriptures of the Supreme Lord is none other than this *spandatattva*;
it is solely by virtue of its own sovereignty that the various forms of its worship are manifested.
In reality, however, everything without exception has this alone as its essential vitality.
As he will say:
"Then, having taken hold of that power, the mantras possess the power of the Omniscient One"—
this too has been demonstrated by way of this method.
And thus, there is no room for any objection to be raised as stated.

In this way, regarding these *Śrī Spandakārikās*, which are like wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*), whatever has been explained by all other commentators and whatever little we ourselves explain, those who are free from envy and devoid of pride will discern the difference for themselves.

Let those of clear intellect investigate this; however, we shall not reveal it by demonstrating it step-by-step, for that would result in excessive prolixity of the text. [Objection: "But surely such a nature is not experienced during states such as waking. And if this [nature] is not suppressed by anyone through the aforementioned reasonings, then the states of waking and so forth will cease of their own accord. To one who, despite this being stated, does not understand the point because of such a doubt, [the author says]: VSpkC_1.2:51. *... [The objection continues... ...if this is not suppressed by anyone through the aforementioned reasonings, then the states of waking and so forth will cease of their own accord. Anticipating this doubt, [the author says]... [The rest of the passage follows].
Awakening [the listener], he teaches:
"Even though it proceeds through the various distinctions of waking and so forth, it does not deviate from its own innate nature as the perceiver, for it remains non-different [from that]. (VSpk 1.3)

The word "jāgrat" (waking), being synonymous with "jāgarā" (awakening), is employed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*). While the distinctions between waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are well-known in the world, or while the states consisting of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*)—
which manifest in various successive forms— are unfolding and flowing forth, [one realizes] that very reality which is inseparable from its own self, the Self of all.
Nor does it ever cease from its nature as the experiencer.

For if it were to cease of its own accord, then even the waking state and so forth, being deprived of that illumination, would not manifest anything at all. Furthermore, this [consciousness's] status as the perceiver is established for everyone through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) in both the waking and dreaming states, even though in deep sleep—

It is not cognized in that manner; nevertheless, it is established by the fact that subsequent memory would otherwise be inexplicable, and because its nature is that of a perceiver, it does not cease to exist. As for the perceived object—such as states [of mind] and so forth—it may well cease through the power of that [perceiver]; what loss is there in this?
The particle *eva* has the sense of "also" (*api*) and its position is displaced; the meaning is that [the nature of Śiva] does not cease even in the absence of those [states].

(VSpkC 1.3:5) The reason for the distinction between waking and so forth is given by way of qualification: "in that which is non-different from that," meaning because they manifest as non-different from that essential nature of Śiva, they are of the nature of light. (VSpkC 1.3:6) And whatever is of one essence with something else—how could that persist when the other has ceased? (VSpkC 1.3:7)
Alternatively, "that" (*yad vā tad*) refers to the agent.
As for the word "undivided" (*abhinna*), it signifies that the non-differentiation of the waking state and so forth exists solely in relation to Śiva.

By implication, even though there is a distinction between the waking states and so forth, that very reality (*tattva*) continues to pervade—that is, it extends and assumes manifold variety—and it should be understood that it never deviates from its own essential nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, this distinction between the waking state and so forth—whether it be considered a transformation (*pariṇāma*) or an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*), as the Sāṃkhyas, Pāñcarātrikas, Grammarians, and others believe—is stated [in the text] as "non-different from that" (*tad-abhinna*) in order to refute such views. Even if the manifoldness of states were to exceed pure consciousness by even the slightest degree, or if the nature of consciousness were to slightly exceed that [manifoldness] during its transformation, then since nothing would remain, there would be no reality at all; therefore, there is no transformation, as it has been said: [The relevant verse: "If the world were different from Brahman, it would not be perceived; If it were non-different, then the world would not exist, nor would Brahman."* Thus, there is no transformation.
"Transformation is not possible for that which is insentient, nor for that which is sentient.
Thus it is said in the venerable *Kiraṇa*.

Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that "transformation" (*vivarta*) consists in the assumption of another form that is distinct and unreal while [the substrate] remains manifest; for if that were so, even the reality of Brahman would necessarily become unreal. Therefore, this definition is also inconsistent.
And by this, the Blessed One’s state of performing what is exceedingly difficult to accomplish has been intimated.

For, while manifesting the distinctions of waking and so forth, He manifests His own non-difference within that very state; thus, He flashes forth in the form of both difference and non-difference—that is, in the nature of the three powers: the lower (aparā), the intermediate (parāpara), and the supreme (parā)—thereby possessing the essence of the six-and-a-half-fold reality of the Anuttara system.
The Blessed One alone vibrates.
Therefore, it is taught that even one who remains in states such as waking and so forth, if they cultivate this very self-nature in this manner and gather [it], they are indeed Śaṅkara.
Now, as for those who say, "We perceive this single form of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*) as the manifold transformations (*vivarta*) of joy, sorrow, and so forth," [it is said]:

The Buddhists maintain that the continuum of consciousness alone is reality; and as for those Mīmāṃsakas who hold that the self is the object of the cognition "I," always obscured by conditions such as pleasure and so forth—he refutes them both with a single verse:
"The cognitions 'I am happy,' 'I am suffering,' and 'I am attached,' etc."
Those [cognitions] clearly exist elsewhere than in that which is permeated by states such as pleasure; for instance:

"I who am happy am the same one who is unhappy," "one is attached because of being joined with passion that underlies pleasure," and "one is averse because of connection with hatred that underlies suffering"—such cognitions and knowings exist "elsewhere," namely, in the self-essence (*ātmatattva*) which is the substratum of those states.

They proceed within that very inward-turned state and clearly come to rest there, having made it their own direct witness. Otherwise, since momentary cognitions are exhausted in themselves alone, conceptual constructions arising from their latent impressions would have no scope for activity regarding what is beyond the range of experience; thus, this synthesis [of experience] would not be possible.
The *ca*s (conjunctions) indicate this synthesis by means of parallelism (*tulyayogitā*).

"In what [state]?"—in that which is otherwise permeated and woven together by states such as pleasure, which arise and perish; that is, in that which remains as the thread of a garland within, permeated by states such as pleasure.

By the word "those" (*tāḥ*), he expresses the fact that the states being connected are objects of memory. Thus, even according to the doctrine of momentary cognition (*kṣaṇika-jñāna-vāda*), although memory—even when colored by the form of the object—is produced from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of experience, it may indeed be similar to that experience.

"Let it be; however, the capacity to establish an object belonging to a past time that has been experienced through experience is not tenable. But when the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) exists as inward-turned within all consciousness, everything becomes consistent. Thus he has indicated. Enough, then, with these discourses which cause distaste for those to be instructed whose hearts are tender.
Those who seek this [truth] should examine recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).
However, since the author himself has merely provided a brief outline of the reasoning here, we have only slightly expanded upon it; therefore, the wise should not be resentful toward us.
For the sake of refuting the Mīmāṃsakas, however, this must be explained in the following manner.

Those cognitions such as "I am happy" and so forth exist—clearly evidenced by worldly consensus—as being woven together (otaprotarūpa) within the subject whose nature is the *puryaṣṭaka* and who is permeated by states such as pleasure; they do not, however, reside in our accepted own-nature (*svasvabhāva*), which is Śiva, a mass of consciousness and bliss. Therefore, [the self] is not always obscured by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of pleasure and the like.
But this Self is composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*).

However, when it remains concealing its own true nature through its innate impurity—which will be described later—then, even in states such as that of the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*), its nature as consisting of happiness and so forth is not obstructed there either; for it has already been stated that its [nature] is not [obstructed] by those [states of] happiness and so forth, and thus it is not obscured by them.
"Whenever [one says], 'I am thin,' 'I am fat,' and so forth— by avoiding such perceptions and instead saying, 'I am happy,' 'I am miserable,' and so on— the intention is this:

by immersing the ground of the *puryaṣṭaka*, which is permeated by the perception of happiness and so forth, into the inward-turned state, one subsequently [attains liberation] through its connection."

Since even external objects such as the body or a jar, through their dissolution, are recognized as having the very nature of Śiva, one must by all means apply effort toward the pacification of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold subtle body). Thus, reiterating the invalidity of all [opposing] doctrines established by the aforementioned reasoning, the preeminent secret Guru— who knows logic, experience, and scripture— proclaims that the reality of Spanda alone exists, as established by valid proof.

Where there is neither suffering nor pleasure, neither the grasped object nor the grasping subject, and even no state of delusion— that exists from the perspective of ultimate reality. In this context,
whatever internal [states] such as suffering or pleasure, or external [objects] such as blue or yellow that are grasped, and that which is the grasper of these— [none of these exist].

To that extent, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), the physical body, the senses, and so forth— which are not being perceived, just as in deep sleep— can clearly be said not to exist. However, when they are indeed perceived, since even these objects of perception consist of consciousness, it follows that only consciousness exists.

As it has been said by our supreme preceptor, the venerable Utpaladeva, who knew the secret of reality, in the *Śrīmad-Īśvarapratyabhijñā*: "The self-luminous [consciousness] is that which illuminates objects; for that which is not luminous cannot be established. (VSpkC 1.5:3–4)
It will also be stated here:
"Because of the realization of identity through the nature of that very cognition" (VSpkC 1.5).
Therefore, where suffering, pleasure, blue, and so forth, as well as their grasper, do not exist, there exists the reality that is a single mass of pure luminosity. (VSpkC 1.5–6)

[Objection: "In that case, when all objects of apprehension (*grāhya*) and subjects of apprehension (*grāhaka*) are annihilated, it follows that the reality (*tattva*) is simply the nature of emptiness (*śūnyātman*). [Reply: He says "no," for he states: "And even the state of delusion (*mūḍhabhāva*) does not exist. The "state of delusion" (*mūḍhabhāva*) is the condition of being deluded; even the form of emptiness (*śūnyarūpatā*) does not exist where this is absent. For how could that which does not manifest at all be said to exist? If it does manifest, then because its very essence is manifestation (*prathātmakatvāt*), it is not something other than manifestation itself. Nor is there ever a state of being (*bhāva*) belonging to manifestation.
For in the absence of that [existence], even the manifestation of its non-existence would be unestablished. And this will be explained later:
"But it is not that which is an inwardly directed state of being."

In this regard: moreover, even that state of delusion— which, though of the nature of Brahman, consists merely in a luminosity devoid of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) whose essence is sovereignty,

and which those who know the Upanishads have realized as "Brahman is consciousness" (*vijñānaṃ brahma*)— even that [state] possesses the power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*) whose essence is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*).
Because [it would otherwise] be insentient, as it has been said in the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"They know that the nature of manifestation is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); otherwise, [it would be inert]."
"Even though consciousness is colored by objects, it remains like an insentient thing, such as a crystal," so it is said.
This is also stated in the *Bhaṭṭanāyaka-stotra*.
"O Lord, how much fruit could this neuter supreme Brahman bear,
were it not for Your manly power as its director, made beautiful by devotion to You?
Thus [it is said].

And thus, from the point where it was stated "that in which it is established" onwards, that very reality which has been investigated exists; and it exists indeed in its ultimate sense, by way of a form established through reasoning, experience, and scripture.
Moreover, it exists in its ultimate sense alone, in a non-constructed and perfect form, but not in a constructed manner like blue and other such objects.
As it has been said by the Great Teachers:
"In this way, these insentient things, which are mere false conceptualizations with respect to the self, exist only as manifestations;
for manifestation alone exists through its own nature and the natures of others. (VSpkC 1.5:16)
Thus [it is said].
And by the venerable Bhartṛhari as well:
"That which is at the beginning, that which is at the end, and that which is in the middle—that alone possesses reality."
"For that which appears, its reality is only to that extent"—
thus [it is said].
Because all sentences possess a restrictive sense (*sāvadhāraṇatva*), the particle *eva* (only/just) should be applied here three times.

Thus, by means of this scripture, having cited as non-existent because they are untenable the views of all those who maintain that there is a continuum of consciousness in forms such as pleasure and so forth; those who maintain that the reality of the subject is defiled by pleasure and so forth; those who maintain a plurality of the grasped and the grasper; those who maintain non-existence; and those who maintain a Brahman that is a mere light devoid of reflective awareness, [the text establishes] the ultimate reality which is precisely the nature of the power of vibration (*spanda*).
It has been asserted that "it exists. Now, however,
within this very reality of vibration (*spandatattva*)— which is the essence of radiance, which is to be cultivated by those of great soul who are attentive to its instruction,
and which manifests— this world consisting of suffering and pleasure, the grasped and the grasper, their absence, and so forth, though it appears to exist, is actually nothing at all for everyone.
Because its sole essence is wonder (*camatkāra*), it has been taught by the great masters that "this very thing exists," such that even sufferings become happiness and even poison becomes nectar.
"And where saṃsāra acts as liberation, that is the path of Śaṅkara. Thus [it is said].
The path of Śaṅkara is the expansion in the form of the supreme power (*parāśakti*), which is the cause for attaining the essential nature of the self of Śaṅkara.
Thus, in order to recognize the reality that has been established through reasoning, he defines the means accompanied by supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*):

"Since this group of instruments, though itself deluded, acts like one who is undeluded, performing the processes of manifestation, maintenance, and withdrawal together with the internal wheel. (VSpk 1.6)
One should diligently and with reverence examine that reality through such effort,
because its independence in all respects is this very unconditioned nature.
(VSpk 1.7) [That reality has been determined with reverence, through faith, and with effort.]

"Exertion (*udyama*) is Bhairava. Thus, one should examine [the reality] by means of that exertion which is of the nature of Bhairava— characterized by the withdrawal of all duality as taught in the *Śivasūtras*, consisting in the expansion of the activity of one's own vital energy (*ojas*), and having as its essence the service of one's own perfectly full, introverted nature.

The phrase "since this [is so]" implies that the innate, natural, and uncreated freedom (*svatantratā*)—which is the very nature of Śiva, self-evident to everyone, and consists of the principle of *spanda*—remains vibrating throughout all objects, whether insentient or sentient.
To the question "What is that reality? he replies with the passage beginning with "since" and ending with "obtains."

"This" refers to that which is well-known in the world as the physical orb (golaka) and so forth, and not that which is established by the scriptures, because the latter is eternally beyond perception and thus cannot be designated as "this. The group of instruments consists of the thirteen organs; being especially deluded under the influence of Māyā, it becomes a semblance of insentience. Having attained a state of delusion even greater than that of the individual soul (aṇu), it nevertheless performs its own activity, maintenance, and withdrawal as if it were undeluded and conscious.
The meaning is that [the soul] attains [objects], becomes oriented toward the sense-objects (*viṣaya*), becomes attached to them, and subsequently withdraws from them.

*How is it together with the "inner wheel" (*antara-cakra*)?* Here, the "inner wheel" refers to the powers of the instruments (*karaṇeśvarī*), not the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), because those are already included by the word "group" (*varga*).
It does not refer to the "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*) to be described later, since the three internal organs situated therein are already covered by the word "group" itself.

Because the subtle elements (*tanmātras*) consist of nothing but latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they cannot be established—relative to a non-yogi—as the direct agents of activity and so forth for whom instruction is intended;
nor can a yogi who has directly realized the subtle elements and is himself absorbed in the contemplation of the supreme reality (*paratattva*) be the recipient of such instruction.
Therefore, this opinion held by some is incorrect.

By the phrase "the deluded one acting like one who is undeluded," only the group of instruments (*karaṇavarga*) is to be connected [with this state], and not even the circle of the Sovereign Goddesses of the Instruments (*karaṇeśvarīcakra*), because that [circle] consists of the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*).

The intention of one who speaks thus is this: that this very nature of Śaṅkara, which performs the most difficult feats through its sovereignty, simultaneously brings about both the essence of consciousness—the circle of the Sovereign Goddesses of the Instruments—and the group of instruments, which takes the form of insentient appearances.

Manifesting as a single unity, She causes the processes of manifestation, maintenance, and withdrawal to proceed; by means of this, the divine sovereigns of the instruments (karaṇeśvarīs) perform their respective creations of entities and so forth, and thus even the insentient group of instruments appears as if it were acting on its own.

Although, according to the secret vision (rahasyadṛṣṭi), there is no insentient group of instruments whatsoever, but rather the sovereigns of the instruments possess bodies of consciousness (vijñānadeha).

Even though they manifest in this way, it is said here that the disciple should be instructed according to well-known conventional understanding and gradually introduced to the teaching on the secret meaning.

And thus, through the sequence beginning with the non-functioning of the group of instruments such as the *golaka* (the physical organs), [one realizes] his own circle of rays (*marīcicakra*) which has the nature of presiding over them.

While performing that very [meditation], one’s own true nature—which consists of the venerable Śaṅkara and impels both [the individual soul and the world]—must be examined; for it is by this very means that it is stated that upon attaining that [nature], this yogin shall possess its unartificial sovereignty (*svatantratā*). This alone is worthy of examination because it is the supreme object to be attained, and it alone can be examined because, according to the reasoning already stated, it is an easy means. Therefore, with earnestness, through the non-restraint of the enjoyment of desired objects—[which is the nature of the practice]— [The text continues: ...by means of the contemplation of the identity of the Self with the Supreme Lord, which is the cause of the cessation of all suffering, the yogin should examine his own true nature, which is the venerable Śaṅkara and the impeller of both [the individual soul and the world]. For it is by this very [contemplation] that it is also stated that, upon attaining that [nature], this yogin shall possess its unartificial sovereignty. This alone is worthy of examination because it is the supreme object to be attained, and it alone can be examined because, according to the aforementioned reasoning, it is an easy means. Precisely for this reason, with reverence, through the non-obstruction of the enjoyment of desired objects—[which constitutes the practice]—[one should proceed].
[This is] out of great respect.
Regarding this, the time for examination has arrived, following the instructions provided here;
as it was said by the secret masters:
"May these functions of my senses, though they may flash forth, fall back into their respective stations;
O Lord, let there never be, even for a moment or in the slightest degree, the audacity of a loss of the flavor of the experience of Your non-duality.
Thus [he prays].

The suffix -kṛtya (here *parīkṣyam*) is used in the sense of fitness (*arhe*), capability (*śakye*), the arrival of the proper time (*prāptakālatāyām*), or as an injunction (*praiṣādau*). Furthermore, by asserting that "the group of insentient instruments obtains activity and so forth through the power of [something else], as if they were not deluded"— an observation witnessed by the experience of everyone— he has thereby also refuted the Cārvāka doctrine which maintains that the senses and other faculties possess consciousness.

Now, how can it be said that "therefore, having attained as it were consciousness from that reality (*tattva*), the sense-faculties themselves obtain activity and so forth," when this very grasper impels the instruments— such as the axe and so on— by his own will? Furthermore, as for what was said, "that reality must be examined with effort," how is that possible, since our desire pursues only external objects and does not proceed toward the examination of reality?
Anticipating the objection that one might "be capable," he says:
"For this [wind] does not function as the impeller of the desire to act;
rather, through contact with its own power, a person becomes equal to it. (VSpk 1.8)

This worldly person does not proceed because of the impulse of desire alone— that is, the goad acting as a catalyst for the operation of the instruments— but rather, through contact with the power of his own conscious nature, which consists of the principle of vibration (*spanda*), he becomes equal to that [power] by means of even a slight immersion (*āveśa*) produced thereby; thus, even though insentient, he attains sentience through the sprinkling of drops from the essence of the I-consciousness (*ahaṃtā*).
It indeed attains [that state].

Then, that reality, having rendered conscious not only the instruments but even the subject—who was merely suspected or imagined as their impeller—makes it itself the recipient of activity and so forth, whereby this conceit arises in him: "I am the instruments."
"I impel [them].

However, even without the penetration of the principle of vibration (*spandatattva*), it is entirely logical that one must examine that very principle which brings about the state of consciousness by penetrating the expansion of the wheel of one's own rays for both the instruments of perception and the perceiver, such that they are no longer "nothing at all.
This is indeed appropriate.

If, on the other hand, one were to claim that the instruments are impelled by another instrument called "will" (*icchā*), which functions like a goad, then that instrument called "will," being itself something to be impelled, would require another instrument for its own impulsion, and that too yet another— resulting in an infinite regress. As for what was said— that "our will does not venture to act upon that"— therein the first half-verse should be accepted [as true], while the latter half should be applied as a subsequent argument.

It is true that this person is not able to initiate a desire for the sake of investigating reality, nor is he capable of making reality the object of his desire, because reality is beyond conceptualization (*avikalpya*). Rather, having pacified the desire that pursues objects by means of their enjoyment, when one [perceives] the inward-turned power of the Self, the principle of vibration (*spandatattva*), which carries consciousness through its own instruments— [The original Sanskrit fragment ends here.]

When one touches [it], then one becomes equal to that; through that immersion (*samāveśa*), one attains autonomy (*svatantratā*) everywhere just like that. Since this is so, the meaning is that reality (*tattva*) must be examined.
(VSpkC 1.8:6) Because the ground of power (*śakti-bhūmi*) primarily consists of touch, it is said: "through the touch of the self's own strength" (VSpkC 1.8:7).

Now, one might object: "Even though this field is composed of the Supreme Lord, why does it not always manifest in its state of perfect plenitude? Why does it depend upon contact with the inward-turned power of the Self? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "When the agitation of one who is incapable due to innate impurity, yet desirous of performing duties, dissolves away, then the supreme state shall be attained. (VSpk 1.9)

One's own innate power of will (*icchā-śakti*), which is manifested through one's own absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) and whose nature is the non-recognition of one's true essence, becomes contracted and takes the form of the "I-am-not-full" (*apūrṇa-manyatā*). This is impurity, the *āṇava* stain. Due to being turbid with the five coverings (*kañcuka*) arising from that stain, the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) gradually undergoes a process of differentiation, culminating in the attainment of the state of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the sense organs, preceded by the states of limited omniscience and partial knowledge.
The impurity of Māyā, which consists of the manifestation of distinct objects through the assumption of extreme limitation, is indeed the impurity of the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
Having first assumed limitations in the form of duality, universal agency, limited agency, and the organs of action, it subsequently attains a state of extreme finitude;
this is also the impurity of Karma, consisting of the performance of auspicious and inauspicious deeds, by means of which [the soul] becomes incapable.

When, for one who possesses the conceptualization of being an agent of primordial knowledge, there is consequently no attainment of desired objects among the worldly and scriptural activities to be performed; when, being perpetually agitated by longing, he does not find rest in his own true nature even for a moment;
then, by virtue of the reasoning and experience already stated and yet to be stated, that agitation—which consists of the egoistic conceit of a subject overwhelmed by desire—[arises].

It would dissolve: preceded by the cessation of the conceit of self in what is not-self, it would dissolve with excellence up to the subsiding of the conceit of non-self in the Self; then its supreme state, consisting of the principle of Spanda, would come to be the object of recognition—this is the meaning.
But it does not arise at that very moment, because of its permanence.
And it is said in the *Vijñānabhairava*:
"The mind, volition, power, and the self—this is the tetrad."
O Beloved, when that [dualistic perception] has completely perished, then that is the form of Bhairava.
Thus [ends the section].

Those who maintain that there exists a distinct substance called "impurity" (mala), denoted by the term "intrinsic impurity" (*nijāśuddhi*), are castigated as being subject to refutation. Now, one might raise the objection: "When the agitation within the nature of the 'I'-consciousness of the subject has subsided, does it not follow that reality is indeed motionless, like a waveless ocean? He dispels this doubt.
Then his uncreated nature, characterized by knowledge and agency, exists;
for by virtue of it, he knows and performs everything that is desired.
[Regarding the word "then" (*tadā*]: with respect to the one to be instructed, the uncreated, innate nature previously described as the form of sovereignty is the very essence of the Supreme Lord.]

The meaning is that at that time, when the agitation has subsided, there occurs for this person the manifestation of that [state] whose defining characteristic is its own nature—namely, knowledge and action—which consist of the essence of Light and Bliss established in a state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) regarding both subjectivity (*jñatva*) and agency (*kartṛtva*). Why is this manifested? He says: because at that moment of entering the supreme state, "everything is desired."
Whatever was desired to be known or whatever was intended to be done by him became manifest at the moment of his entry; he both knows that very thing and performs it.
Here, the two occurrences of the particle *ca* indicate simultaneity; however, as some claim, they do not suggest the identity of knowledge and action.
For that [identity] has already been established by the single qualifying attribute "characterized by being a knower and an agent," which points to the subject through its defining characteristics.
This was stated by the one who expresses the true nature [of reality]:

"Now, because of the firm support of the *spanda-tattva*— which is directly realized through the stabilization of the process of unfolding (*unmeṣa*) as set forth in the aphorism 'Then, from the instrument' and 'one's own impurity'— even for one who makes even the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*) of a single flavor with meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there is the severance of worldly existence (*bhava*)."
Thus he says:
"For one who, beholding that intrinsic nature as the state of the presiding subject, remains as if smiling, from where could this crooked path arise? (VSpk 1.11)

Observing and reflecting upon that innate nature of his own, which consists of the principle of *spanda* (vibration), recognized through reasoning, perception, repeated practice, and recognition, and which pervades him as the presiding subject even during the state of worldly emergence (*vyutthāna*),
[the yogi realizes: "The power, in the form of the vital breath (*marut*), does not go out nor enter when it is expanded."
"By means of that non-conceptuality in the center, one assumes the form of Bhairava"—thus it is said. Likewise:
"All powers, such as perception and the rest, [emerge] simultaneously and in all directions from the mind toward their respective objects of knowledge."
"Having cast [all things] into the center, standing as a pillar of gold, you alone shine forth in the form of the universe.
According to the logic of the tradition taught in this *Śrī-Vijñānabhairavakakṣyāstotra*, by means of the samādhi of closing and opening [the eyes],

and through the simultaneous support of the pervasive middle ground, one whose every conceptual construction has dissolved— the forest of emission consisting of both [subject and object] having been transcended— [shines forth].
With the wheel of the senses expanded in succession:
with the internal as the object of focus and the gaze directed outward, free from the opening and closing of the eyes—
this is that Bhairavī Mudrā, concealed in all the Tantras.

Thus, having entered the mudrā of the Lord Bhairava as traditionally taught, he beholds the vast multitude of objective phenomena—which, like a collection of various reflections sinking and emerging within a mirror, arise in the very sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) and dissolve back into that same space. Through the recognition of his own extraordinary, innate nature—a mass of supreme bliss unprecedented throughout thousands of births—he suddenly severs all mental fluctuations. Smiling, as if entered into the mudrā of wonder (*vismayamudrā*), he attains a state of great expansion.

And for that lord of yogins who remains—having suddenly attained his true, inherent nature—he does not become slackened by any external support; for him, this wretched course of worldly activity (*sṛti*), which causes the entire world to tremble and consists of the continuous succession of birth, death, and so forth, how could it possibly exist? The meaning is that it certainly does not occur, because its cause—the characteristic of one's own impurity—is absent.
As it is said in the Śrīpūrvaśāstra:
"But one whose mind is unwavering in reality, even while enjoying sense objects, is not touched by defects at all, just as a lotus leaf is not touched by water. (VSpkC 1.11:6)
"Just as one who is protected by mantras and the like that remove poison does not lose consciousness even while consuming poison, so too is the yogi of great intelligence. // VSpkC_1.11:7–8 //

Now, in order to awaken those such as the followers of the Upanishads, Akṣapāda (the Naiyāyikas), and the Mādhyamikas— who have taught that at the dissolution of the cosmic agitation, only a reality consisting of non-existence remains in the form of universal annihilation— the author defines the *spanda-tattva*, the body of this treatise, as being supramundane by way of its opposition to the reality accepted by them.
Non-existence cannot be brought into being, nor is there any lack of delusion regarding it;
for through contact with diligent application, there arises the certainty that "it existed [previously]."

Therefore, that should always be known as artificial, like the state of deep sleep; for it does not attain the status of reality merely by being remembered. (VSpk 1.13) "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent. (VSpkC 1.12–13)

By such statements as these, it is shown that non-existence (*abhāva*), which is favored by those who know the Upanishads and others, cannot become an object of cultivation (*bhāvya*). This is because cultivation has as its object a thing to be cultivated (*bhāvya-vastu*), whereas non-existence is nothing at all; or, if it were to be cultivated, it would possess some reality and thus would no longer be non-existence. Furthermore, where there is the non-existence of even the one who cultivates (*bhāvaka*), that would be the annihilation of the universe—how could such a thing be cultivated? But if the existence of the cultivator is admitted, then there is no annihilation of the universe.
Because the meditator (bhāvaka) remains [as a residual entity], it is not the case that the non-existence of the universe (*viśvābhāva*) alone is reality.

Now, suppose this position is held: "This meditator is a conceptual construct (*kalpita*); while cultivating the total annihilation of the universe as constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), upon the completion of that cultivation, he becomes of the nature of non-existence due to his identity with the object of cultivation (*bhāvya*).
To this, it is replied: In that cultivation of non-existence, there is no non-delusion (*amūḍhatā*); nor is there non-delusion therein, but rather there is only delusion (*moha*).
"Whatever is intensely meditated upon,
when that meditation reaches completion, results in a clear conceptual cognition"—
according to this principle, if one meditates on non-existence in the form of the annihilation of the universe, the ultimate truth is never attained.
Now it is said:
It is empty of all objective phenomena and all principles without exception, as well as of all latent tendencies of the afflictions; yet, from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is not empty.
Thus, as stated by Nāgārjuna, that is what is called "emptiness.

If one were to accept a ground that is a mass of consciousness-bliss (*cidānandaghana*), autonomous, ultimate, and serving as the foundational substratum—as is taught in the *Vijñānabhairava* and other texts regarding the Supreme Goddess who transcends the calculations of space and time—then [the following would apply].

By such statements as these, having established the ultimate ground of consciousness (*cidbhūmi*), which serves as the foundation, the meditation on emptiness (*śūnyabhāvanā*) is taught; otherwise, this expression "emptiness" would not be [meaningful], because it has been demonstrated that "whatever is intensely meditated upon becomes that very thing.
As for that which was said: [VSpkC_1.12-13:10]
"That state which is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is something unknowable to those like me;
it does not, however, follow the sense of nihilism as it is commonly understood in the world.
This is stated in the *Ālokamālā*. That is true: for those like you, it is unknowable, and because it is unknowable, it is impossible to describe.

Let it be said: "What is emptiness? But how so? For as long as even emptiness is being cultivated, it must be avoided by the discerning, because it is still inscribed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
And if that [emptiness] cannot be known by those such as you, then one should perform service to a true guru who possesses direct realization of that state.
However, one should not, by means of mere personal fancy, engage in discourse that casts oneself and others into the bottomless great delusion of [claiming] "it is emptiness"—enough of this!
Now, from where is it known that there is delusion in that regard? To this, he provides the answer with the words "since" (*yataḥ*).
*Abhiyoga* is the verbal expression consisting of an inquiry directed toward that state— such as "What was I like when I arose from meditative absorption?"—

and the certainty that "It was so" arising from contact with it and by virtue of it; because there is the realization, "I was profoundly deluded," that very state of delusion is thus postulated, since it is being remembered and because it was experienced.
On the contrary, [the witness-consciousness] makes known the very existence of the experiencer, the knower, who is of the nature of a persisting subject, and not its non-existence; thus,
it is stated that even in the state where the universe is absent, the form of consciousness remains entirely unimpaired, and therefore its non-existence can never be asserted.

[Objection: But surely, what has been seen—that is, ascertained—is remembered as blue and so forth; yet there is no ascertainment of that which has become void and whose cognitive activity has subsided. Therefore, how can it be said that "that was [there]"? [Reply: That is merely confusion regarding subsequent ascertainments. It is said in response: This is the nature of the object of cognition (*vedya*), because this essence consisting of "this-ness" (*idantā*)—to the extent that it is elevated into the self of the cognizer by way of its own "this-ness"—[is what is remembered].

Since that which is not determined cannot be remembered, and because the cognizer—even when contracted during states such as the imagined void—is in reality the non-conventional ultimate *ahaṃ* (I-consciousness), there is no separateness within its own self; thus, the conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) that determines it has as its object only that which is reflected upon as "I. At that time, the form of the void-cognizer is not established at all in self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), and because it is the correlate of the universe, its essence consists of contraction.

There is no inconsistency whatsoever in the fact that it is remembered at a time subsequent [to its experience], because for this reason that state (*pada*), whose nature is void, is artificial. Therefore, according to the very principle stated [in the verse]: "Whatever, whether real or unreal, is intensely meditated upon," it has been brought forth by the Supreme Lord through the meditation on the unreal (*abhūtabhāvanā*) for the sake of concealing knowledge; the meaning is that it was manifested in such a way as an object of attainment for the deluded. The object of knowledge (*jñeya*), that which is to be known, and the form of the object of knowledge are always like deep sleep; this is the illustration.

The intended meaning is this: this state of being is always in deep sleep, consisting of delusion, and is established without effort; it exists in everyone. Therefore, what is the use of this other [state] acquired through the exertion of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), since there is no difference between the two in their lack of substantial reality? Furthermore, most of those who have entered this difficult-to-cross ocean of great delusion—namely, the Vedāntins, the followers of Akṣapāda (Nyāya), the Sāṃkhyas, the Sugatas (Buddhists), and others—are situated within this very void.
And for those who desire to enter the reality of vibration (*spandatattva*) but whose effort has become slackened, this void becomes an obstacle.
As he will say:
"Then, in that great void..."
Beginning with these words, up to:
"The fool is like one in the state of deep sleep" (VSpkC 1.12–13).
Therefore, a great intensity of effort is observed on the part of the author regarding its eradication.
Thus, although it has already been determined here as something to be abandoned, it will be determined once more:
that which is an effort directed toward an effect.
Regarding this:

"Therefore, since we have undertaken this refutation, your honors should not feel anger toward us, having lent your ears to our examination of the instruction. When the followers of the Sugata have been refuted, those who propound the Upaniṣads and so forth are also necessarily refuted, as the logic is the same; thus, nothing further has been said.

Now we shall speak precisely of the subject at hand: that reality called *spanda* does not, in this way, attain the state of being remembered like the void (*śūnya*), because it is impossible for that which is of a single nature—perpetually and continuously perceived by the perceiver—to ever be unperceived.
And so they have said:
"By what means, O Maitreyī, could one know the knower?
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.15).

Even though the state of absorption is remembered by one who has emerged from it due to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, nevertheless, it is not merely that much.
The reality of vibration (*spandatattva*), moreover, is precisely that supreme subject whose essence consists of the light and bliss that are all-pervasive and undivided.
As he will say:
"Therefore, among all reflections upon words and their meanings, there is no state that is not Śiva."
Thus [ends the section]. VSpkC 1.12–13:35:
Therefore, for this [Reality], whose nature is uninterrupted wonder, there can never be the state of being remembered or the state of being deluded.
VSpkC 1.12–13:36–37: As for the fact that it is referred to here by the word "that" (*tat*) in the phrase "that Reality" (*tattattva*), that [is as follows]:
"Having [conceived] the Self as liberated through its own sovereignty" (VSpkC 1.12–13)—
according to the principle stated in the *Śrīpratyabhijñākārikā*, this refers only to that which is imagined and lacks an ultimate nature, and not to that which is in reality ultimate.
By the phrase "does not realize," he means that there is no cognition whatsoever of this reality by way of being remembered.

Now, one might raise this objection: "In passages such as 'wherein it is situated' (*yatra sthitam*), it was stated that the very nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) assumes the form of the manifold effects of the universe; yet you have not grasped that artificial, non-existent form produced by meditation. Therefore, how can its state of being unconfused (*amūḍhatva*) consist in a form of uninterrupted wonder? To this doubt, he says: [VSpkC 1.12–13:41]
And here, there are two states designated as "the state of being an effect" and "the state of being an agent.
Among these, the state of being an effect is perishable, whereas agency is imperishable.
Only that effort which is directed toward an object is lost here;
when that is lost, the ignorant person thinks, "I am destroyed."
But as for that inward-turned state which is the locus of the quality of omniscience,
its loss could never occur, because nothing else is perceived.
*In this context of the *Spanda-tattva*, there exists a pair of states differentiated merely by linguistic convention, designated as "being an effect" and "being an agent."

In reality, that single principle— which is Śiva, a mass of independent light— is pervaded by an activity whose nature is light and which is non-different from the existence of the agent; manifesting as non-distinct from that [agent], it assumes the form of the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), bodies, and their absences, and is thus called the "effect" (*kārya*), because nothing else can possibly possess causality.
As it is said in the *Śrīpratyabhijñā*:
"But for that which is insentient, there is no such power by which the non-existent becomes existent;
therefore, the nature of cause and effect consists precisely in the relationship of agent and object. (VSpkC 1.14–16)
Thus:

"And its very nature as an effect (*kāryatva*) consists in this: that it joins and disjoins, in a sequential manner, the infinite appearances of bodies, blue objects, and so forth—which, though not distinct from the essential nature of the conscious self (*cidātman*), appear as if distinct like reflections in a mirror—by means of various appearances of place, time, and other such factors."
Whatever it manifests, and however much it manifests, all of that—precisely because it is being manifested—exists in an outward-turned form characterized by the nature of decay;

and its decay consists in the submergence of the manifestation of "this-ness" (idantā) and its persistence in the form of "I-ness" (ahantā). For this very reason, only that objective portion belonging to the subject—the body and so forth—is created and withdrawn by the Lord, but not that which consists of the light of "I-ness."

Because its nature as the agent remains solely that of the Lord even when it enters into bodies and so forth, therefore, between those two— being the object and being the agent— the state of being the object is perishable, whereas agency, which consists of the freedom of consciousness, is imperishable; for even during the arising and passing away of the world, it does not deviate from its own nature.

But if there were movement, neither the arising nor the passing away of the world would manifest; therefore, even in states such as delusion, this [consciousness] remains undeluded, its essence being the unimpeded power of wonder (*camatkāra*).

[Objection: Surely we do not perceive its agency in deep sleep and similar states where non-existence is established, since no activity whatsoever is observed there. [Reply: True. That which is effort (*prayatna*)—the impetus (*saṃrambha*) consisting of the operation directed toward the senses and so forth, tending toward the production of an effect—is what is meant here.

Thus, in this state where activity has ceased, it is dissolved and cut off; when that has been dissolved, the ignorant one—whose own nature has been carried away by the meditative absorption of non-existence (abhāva-samādhi)—being deluded, thinks, "I am annihilated.
Furthermore, that intrinsic nature which is inward-turned and consists of the manifestation of the "I-sense" (ahaṃtā) is, for that very reason, the locus of the quality of omniscience.

And this is an illustrative indication [of a further point]: even the loss of its status as the agent of all things and so forth could never occur; for it is not conceivable that such a loss ever happens, since no other entity capable of perceiving such a loss is ever perceived. If some such entity were perceived, it would be none other than this very one whose nature is consciousness turned inward (*antarmukha-cid-rūpa*). If, however, it is not perceived, then how can there be any certainty that a state of its loss exists?
Moreover, since no one else perceives its absence, but rather that very self-luminous entity itself [is perceived], how can there be its non-existence?
Thus, in the phrase "because another is not perceived," the meaning is "because the perception by another agent is absent.
Furthermore, just as the absence of a jar is determined by the perception of the ground or other objects devoid of the jar, so too is the absence of the self [determined].
Since nothing devoid of a self is ever perceived, one might conclude that the existence of the perceiver must necessarily follow from that perception;
thus, the non-existence of the perceiving self is not established.

Furthermore, if [the self] were to perish upon the cessation of the effort directed toward an effect, then no other person would perceive anything thereafter, which would entail the absurd consequence that there is no perception by anyone else. This is the meaning.

Moreover, since another effort directed outwardly is not perceived during states such as deep sleep, how could the ignorant suspect the destruction of reality, which is inwardly directed? For when one thing is destroyed, what happens to the other? Furthermore, because another effort directed toward an effect is not perceived, and because this non-perception is manifest, [reality] is never [destroyed].

There is no disappearance of that perceiver who is of the nature of light and turned inward; for since this state of being inward-turned is the locus of the quality of omniscience, one indeed perceives even that state of non-existence [of objects], otherwise that very state could not be established. The genitive case in "anyasya" (of another) is used in the sense of both the agent and the object.

*In the state of being turned inward (*antarmukha*), the status of the agent (*kartṛtva*) is said to be a "possible condition" (*sambhāvyāvasthātva*), just like the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of being an object (*kāryatva*).
