But in reality, according to the reasoning already stated, it is precisely its status as the abider (*avasthātṛtva*).

Regarding the term "turned inward" (*antarmukha*): it should be construed as that whose "mouth" (*mukha*), meaning the primary [aspect], consists of the fullness of the I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) within.

Thus, when the outward-directed activity has ceased, the unawakened person perceives even the self (*ātman*), which is the grasper (*grāhaka*), as non-existent—even though such non-existence is logically untenable.
Having thus established that "one should ascertain," he now defines the nature of the perception of the Self for both the well-awakened and the unawakened:
"The perception of that [Self] is constant and never deviates from the three states;
it belongs eternally to the well-awakened, whereas for another, it occurs at the beginning and end [of those states]. (VSpk 1.17)

The perception of that fundamental nature— which is uninterrupted luminosity— by virtue of the reasoning already stated, belongs to one who is perfectly awakened and devoid even of the latent impressions of non-awakening; it is constant throughout all three states of waking,
dreaming, and deep sleep, eternal in its beginning, middle, and end, unerring and imperishable, and indeed always exists as his own essential nature, which is Śiva.
The meaning is that it "throbs" (sphurati).

Furthermore, for another who is unawakened, regarding each of those ten [energies] which consist of their own appropriate forms of consciousness, there is an inward-turning characterized by repose at both the beginning—when they desire to emerge—and at the end; however, this does not occur in the intermediate state, which consists of the abiding in the manifestation of objects appropriate to them.
As it is stated in the *Śrīśivadṛṣṭi*:

"Even in those states where there is contact with the knower who is the foremost of all knowers, that [consciousness] is perceived as remaining present, either through rest in that [object] or in the fruit. (VSpkC 1.17)

*Bhaṭṭa Lollaṭa also explained [the verse] in his own commentary exactly as "at its beginning and end" (*tad-ādyante*). Relying on the words of the commentary by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa, we too—untrained in interpreting the meaning of the Sūtra through strained constructions, even though it is exceedingly clear—have followed the words of that commentary; for this very reason, [it is said] "at the beginning and end of that" (*tad-ādyante*) for one who is not well-awakened.
Since there is the perception of that [reality], for this very reason, this qualified person is here awakened to perfect enlightenment by means of the teachings on Spanda.
As he will say:
"Therefore, one should be constantly diligent for the sake of discerning the reality of Spanda."
"Waking," and so forth;
like the state of deep sleep, when one is deluded, one becomes awakened and unenveloped.
Thus; likewise even in a dream;
and so forth.
"One should always remain awakened," and so forth.
For here, among the three states beginning with waking, even the middle state— just like the initial and final limits— is essentially characterized by the determination of objects.

The instruction has begun in order to bring about the state of being "well-awakened" for one who is already awakened, so as to make [the mind] consist of the enjoyment of the Fourth State (turyābhoga); and we shall establish this point.
And likewise, the Śivasūtra states:
The experience of the fourth state (*turya*) arises within the distinctions of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
likewise,
the fourth should be poured into the three like oil.
Thus:
"The enjoyer of the triad is the Lord of Heroes (vīreśa).
Thus [ends the commentary on verse 1.17].
He demonstrates, by way of analysis, the nature of the perception that occurs for Suprabuddha in the three stages:

"Endowed with the supreme power whose nature consists of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, the All-pervasive Lord shines forth in two stages; but in the stage other than those, He consists of pure consciousness alone. (VSpk 1.18)

For one who is perfectly awakened, the pervasive nature whose essence is Śaṅkara— the self-nature endowed with the supreme power (parāśakti) which is the very essence of Spanda— shines forth in the two states of waking and dreaming as the middle state, characterized by the abundance of the nature of both knowledge and the object of knowledge; however, in the states at the beginning and end of that knowledge, it shines through its own essential nature alone.

For in that state, he perceives the universe like Sadāśiva and Īśvara, as his own limbs; but elsewhere, in deep sleep (*suṣupta*), it is not as others perceive it in both deep sleep and the fourth state (*turya*). Since the discussion has commenced with the phrase "the three states are non-deviating," the fourth state is not the subject at hand, and because the perception of that [state] itself constitutes the nature of the fourth. Thus, this all-pervading one shines for him as consisting of consciousness alone, due to the cessation of all objects of knowledge.

This [statement] reflects the intention of Suprabuddha alone and does not follow the actual state of things; for otherwise, the claim that [the self] is "consisting of consciousness" (*cinmaya*) would become untenable elsewhere, since in the world the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*) consists of delusion (*moha*), whereas from the perspective of Śiva, even the waking and dreaming states consist of consciousness. Even so, this would still be irrelevant to the subject at hand.

*From this point until the end of the first *niḥṣyanda*, the text stands for the sake of the fully awakened one’s state of being well-awakened; just as it was not noticed by the commentators, let it be examined by oneself.
How much shall we write at every single step?
[VSpkC_1.18:3] He demonstrates how even these intermediate states, such as waking and so forth, do not obstruct the one who is awakened. [VSpkC_1.18:4]
The outflows of the vibration of the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, having attained their self-nature by relying upon the universal vibration, will never be obstacles for the knower.

[Note: The "qualities" (*guṇa*) are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Here, that which is intended is the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*), which exists as the principle of illusion (*māyā-tattva*) within the sphere of manifestation.]
As it is stated in the *Śrī-svacchanda* [Tantra], in the section on the arrangement of the *māyā-masūra-kava*:
"One should contemplate the covering below as red and that above as white;
one should know that darkness (*tamas*) is in the middle—these are the qualities (*guṇa*) thus established. (VSpkC 1.19:2)
Thus:

those [energies] beginning with *kalā* and ending with *pṛthivī*, which are specific expansions of movement (*spanda*), and their outflows—the expansions of the body, organs, and worlds, as well as cognitions such as blue and pleasure—and likewise, according to the capacity [of the practitioner], the *bindu*, *nāda*, and so forth; all these belong eternally to the knower who is perfectly awakened.
The certainty is that for someone whose birth is indeed their last and who is free from obstacles, these [impurities] do not become obscurers of one's own true nature; for,

having attained their self-nature through the perspective determined by the fact that they abide by relying upon the form liberated from common vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*), they have arisen from that very source and consist of that— this is the meaning.
For instance:

"The knowledge and action of the Lord regarding entities that are His own limbs, with Māyā as the third, are precisely what constitute the *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* of the bound soul (*paśu*). (VSpkC 1.19)

Thus, according to the view expressed in the *Śrī-Pratyabhijñā*, the sovereign power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) itself, manifesting as the triad of powers— knowledge, action, and *māyā*— in the state of Śrī Sadāśiva and others, assumes a body of play (*krīḍāśarīra*) consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* through the intensification of contraction (*saṃkoca*). Consequently,
because everything is always permeated by the expansion of its own power of consciousness, the fully awakened one (*suprabuddha*) knows everything while presiding over it.
Even while not severing the fluctuations of specific qualities and so forth, one remains entirely absorbed in the reality of Spanda.
[VSpkC_1.19:7] However, it is explained how these [fluctuations] bind those who are unawakened:
"But for those of unawakened intellect, these [fluctuations] strive to conceal their own true state."
They cause [beings] to fall onto the terrible path of saṃsāra, which is so difficult to cross.

These aforementioned qualities and so forth are the outflows of the vibration (*spanda*) [of consciousness], [affecting] those whose intellect is generally unawakened— namely, worldly people who identify the body as the self because they do not recognize their own *spanda*-principle as being essentially the power of the Supreme Lord, as well as practitioners of limited yoga who identify the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and other such factors as the self.

Constantly striving to conceal their own state, which is the essence of the principle of vibration (*spanda*), and having that very effort as their sole substance, they cause the wheel of living beings to fall upon this terrible, sorrowful path of saṃsāra— a path so difficult to traverse that it cannot be crossed, and from which sentient beings are rescued with great hardship by the teachers.
As it is said in the Śrīmālinīvijaya:

"Those [powers] which, embracing the Rudra-aṇus who are completely absorbed in sense objects, cause them to fall lower and lower, are known as the Apara (Lower) powers, who are most terrible. (VSpkC 1.20:2)
Thus [it is said].

For that very Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), whose essence is the principle of vibration (*spandatattva*) as previously established, is the Power Vāmeśvarī because she emits (*vamana*) the universe both internally and externally, and because she follows the left-hand path (*vāmācāra*) of transmigratory existence; and those forms—Khecarī, Gocarī, Dikcarī, and Bhūcarī—are raised up by her.

The four wheels of the deities (*devatācakra*) lead those who are well-awakened to traverse the supreme planes, whereas for those who are unawakened, they impel them along progressively lower paths. For indeed, those very goddesses (*khecarī*) who move in the sky of consciousness (*bodhagagana*) for the well-awakened—being the causes for the manifestation of timelessness, non-duality, universal agency, omniscience, fullness, and pervasiveness—exist for the unawakened as the state of the empty subject (*śūnyapramātṛ*). Abiding in the form of coverings (*kañcuka*), they become the causes for limitation through the attachment to being limited by time, limited agency, and limited knowledge.

Speech is the "cow" (*gauḥ*). Moving within the stages of intellect, ego, and mind—which are characterized by that [speech] and consist of discursive thought—the "movements" (*gocaryāḥ*) produce for the well-awakened one determinations, conceits, and volitions consisting of non-difference from one's own self; but for the deluded, they produce those whose sole essence is difference.

(VSpkC 1.20:6) Moving within the ten directions, which are the stages of the external senses, the "directional movements" (*dikcaryāḥ*) have the manifestation of non-duality as their essence for the well-awakened one, whereas for others, they are the causes for the manifestation of duality. (VSpkC 1.20:7)

The sphere of objects of knowledge (*meyapada*) consists of the fivefold [elements] beginning with earth and form; moving within that sphere are the *bhūcaryas*. At that time, through the state of solidification (*āśyānībhāva*) of that which consists of enjoyment (*bhoga*), they have attained identity with it. As the *bhūcaryas*, they manifest themselves as the body of the light of consciousness for the well-awakened one, while for others they remain manifesting limitation in every respect. Thus, [the world] exists precisely in the form of the knower, the internal organ, the external organs, and the objects of knowledge.

Those four wheels, consisting of the vibration of the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, cause worldly people of unawakened intellect, as well as yogins who are satisfied merely with the manifestation of the *bindu*, *nāda*, and so on, to fall into this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which consists of the expansion of those respective principles (*tattva*).
Since it is thus: [VSpkC_1.20:9]

Therefore, one who is constantly engaged in discerning the reality of Spanda attains their own true nature even while awake, before long. (* "Constantly engaged" means intent upon the discernment— that is, the reflective awareness— of the reality of Spanda, which consists of what has been said and what is yet to be said.)

"Those who, fixing their minds on me, worship me with constant discipline"— according to this view expressed in the *Gītā*, he who is perpetually inclined toward contemplating his own inward-turned nature attains, even while awake and remaining in the waking state,
his own innate nature which is Śiva, and thus his very self becomes Śiva.

The meaning is that the internal nature itself emerges spontaneously, by which one becomes awakened; through the attainment of the ever-arisen immersion (*samāveśa*), one becomes well-awakened and liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*).

Just as for one who is thus engaged, there occurs the certain cessation of all other mental fluctuations—which arise under the influence of powerful objects—consisting of effortless [absorption] and its opposite.
To teach that those states in which the application of effort remains unsealed, open, and present are the primary objects of exertion, he says:
"Whether extremely angry or exceedingly joyful, or reflecting, 'What shall I do? [VSpkC 1.21:3]
Or whatever step one may take while running, therein the *spanda* is established.
(VSpk 1.22) In all cases on the path of means (*upāyamārga*), yogins first bring about the cessation of all other mental fluctuations and then become one-pointed;

even in these states such as extreme anger and the like—which consist of the destruction of all other fluctuations—[they do so] by their own natural force (*svarasataḥ*) for the sake of discerning the reality of *spanda*.

The yogins who are constantly diligent turn inward instantaneously; they obtain that which they desire in no time at all. The intended meaning is that those who are not yogins are indeed deluded in this regard. For instance, [this is evident] from seeing an enemy who has just inflicted a terrible injury, or from hearing words that strike one's vital points.

Or, at the very first moment, by the power of the deity of the desire to withdraw [the senses] as they begin to open, his circle of rays turns inward; he becomes either intensely enraged, or—upon seeing the moon-like face of the mistress of his life long sought—he becomes overjoyed, his entire circle of sensory organs expanding and rushing forward under the influence of the deity of fully arisen longing; or, due to being hemmed in on all sides by the force of a powerful assailant, he becomes terrified and bewildered, wondering, "What shall I do?"

Whether one has entered into a state of self characterized by ascending streams of doubt through conceptualization; or whether, with all objective supports exhausted, the expansion of mental activity has been rendered supportless as blossoming doubt-consciousness ceases;

or whether, pursued by a mad elephant and the like, one is running with no regard for the body, possessed by the act of fleeing most swiftly due to the impulsion of the Goddess of Effort, whose other mental activities have been turned toward the Self;
or likewise in other such states, such as those produced by great terror upon seeing a lion, a python, or similar things—whatever [occurs therein].

One should go to and abide in that state which consists in the cessation of mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*). For that person among yogins who is constantly striving for the discernment of the reality of *spanda*, *spanda* is established in that particular state consisting of the cessation of fluctuations;
the reality of *spanda* remains as if directly present before him.

Therefore, having recognized this state as the cessation of mental fluctuations, the yogi— possessing the awareness of his own innate power of vibration (*spanda*) which has become manifest— should either immediately pacify the fluctuations of anger and doubt by means of the technique of contracting the limbs like a tortoise, or expand the fluctuations of joy and running by means of the technique of great expansion and pervasion; [in either case], fear [is transcended].
As it is said in the venerable Vijñānabhairava:
"When the intellect has been made motionless within the sphere of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy, that reality remains. (VSpkC 1.22:5)

When great joy is attained, or when a kinsman is seen after a long time, one should contemplate that arisen joy; becoming absorbed in it, one’s mind should become fixed upon it. Even in the face of fear at the end of hunger and so forth, in grief, or in a deep abyss or a rushing torrent, [one should remain thus].
"In curiosity, at the end of hunger and so forth, the existence of Brahman is near.
Thus, having first cultivated the power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*) in these states through the stated reasoning, and subsequently maintaining one's connection with that very power—

"One who is constantly diligent should bring about the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), which consists of entering into the firmness of that [realization] in all circumstances"—thus he instructs.
"Having formed the resolve: 'Whatever this [teacher] shall say to me, having taken hold of that state, I will certainly do it,' one should remain [in that state]. (VSpk 1.23)
Relying upon that [channel], both the moon and the sun set within the path of the *suṣumṇā* by way of the upward path,
leaving behind the domain of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).

Then, in that great void where the moon and sun have dissolved, the deluded one becomes awakened and unobscured, like the state of deep sleep. This is my own nature, which Śaṅkara will declare; it is that which, when manifested, is a mass of consciousness and bliss.

Having formed the resolve and reached a firm decision, thinking, "My own nature, previously experienced, will examine me; therefore, I shall certainly act accordingly, abandoning outward-turnedness and becoming solely intent upon that," he remains with the movement of conceptual thought stilled, relying upon and aiming for that state which consists of the vibration of the mass of consciousness-bliss— a state previously experienced even in conditions of extreme anger and the like.

The yogi who dwells in the non-conceptual state with unwavering steadiness—relying upon that very state—the moon and the sun, namely both the *apāna* and the *prāṇa*, having met together in the region of the heart, simultaneously set and subside by way of the upward path of the *udāna* through the *suṣumnā* channel, the *brahmanāḍī*. How so? By abandoning the objective field characterized by the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*).
Having abandoned the maṇḍala presided over by Brahmā, who is the presiding deity of the *brahmabila*, and having relinquished the pervasion of the body up to the upper lid [of the cranial aperture],

one then reaches the Great Void— the supreme ether which consists in the cessation of all objects of knowledge— wherein the moon and sun, in their aforementioned forms, have become intensely dissolved because the pervasion of the body has been transcended; yet, even upon reaching that, he who [remains] due to slackened effort...

Because one is deluded by the outflow of the vibration of the qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth through the nature of *khecarī* and the rest, one becomes like the state of deep sleep (*sauṣupta*). By "deep sleep," even the state of dreaming is implied; thus, like the states of dreaming and deep sleep, that yogi who presides over the stages of emptiness (*śūnya*) and so forth is called "deluded" (*mūḍha*), as his own true nature remains completely unmanifest.
As it was said by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa:
"By relying upon that state whose essence is vibration"—
thus [it is said] of the yogins.
And thus:
he whose manifestation of his own intrinsic nature has not occurred properly would, being deluded by dreams and the like, remain unawakened and suppressed. Thus.

But he who, even in that state, does not slacken for even a moment due to the strength of his exertion and the power of his effort, is said to be "awakened" (*prabuddha*), because he remains as the very nature of the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) and is not overcome by darkness. For this very reason, the teachers have instructed that the yogi must be one who possesses constant exertion. May there be auspiciousness!
The *Spandakārikā*, second outflow:
Having seized that power, mantras possess the power of the Omniscient One.
They proceed for the sake of [fulfilling] their respective functions, like the sense organs of embodied beings.
Right there they are completely dissolved, tranquil in form and stainless;
together with the mind of the worshipper, these possess the nature of Śiva.
(*Having seized that power consisting of the reality of Spanda, which is the vital breath, as its essence, and having firmly established it as a non-dual support.)

The Blessed Ones—the mantras such as Anantavyomavyāpin and others—by means of their omniscient power and their capacity for omniscience and so forth, being praised and expanding, proceed for the sake of the empowerment of embodied beings; that is to say, they perform creation, withdrawal, concealment, grace, and so on. // VSpkC_2.1:1 //
The term "omniscient" (*sarvajña*) emphasizes the state of being [the essence] and indicates [attributes] such as being the agent of all things.

(VSpkC 2.1:2) Just as the sense organs of embodied beings, having been brought forth by that vision and having taken hold of its power, proceed toward the illumination of objects and so forth—this is the illustration.

(VSpkC 2.1:3) Likewise, those who are stainless, because they have accomplished what was to be done and whose impurities of office have ceased, possess the nature of the Self which is the peaceful and distinguished denoter. (VSpkC 2.1:3)

In that very power whose nature is vibration (*spanda*), they dissolve completely through the attainment of non-differentiation, pre-eminently and without returning; they are liberated from further impurities along with the mind of the worshipper and the consciousness of the world of devotees.
As it has been said:
"Having favored the multitude of individual souls, they have gone to the state that is free from affliction.
(VSpkC 2.1:5) Thus it is said.

And because they have arisen from that very source and are emitted by its power, they dissolve back into that same place; therefore, these [beings], such as the mantras and the lords of mantras (*mantreśvara*), [are so designated].

Those who possess a nature (*dharma*) or inherent essence related to Śiva, the Supreme Lord, are "such" (*tathā*); the meaning is that they have the essential nature of universal vibration (*sāmānyaspanda*).
[Objection: Now, since the emergence and so forth of the instruments (*karaṇas*) and the mantras are equal, why is it that the instruments do not possess forms such as omniscience and the rest?

It is said that the Supreme Lord, by means of his power of *māyā*, fashions bodies and instruments consisting of duality; but by means of his power of *vidyā*, he [fashions] the *mantras*, whose bodies consist of the various reflective awarenesses (*parāmarśa*) of denotators belonging to the realm of space.
Even in the state of *māyā*, there is a denotator;
for the determination "this is a jar" exceeds [mere] name and form.
"‘The power of the Supreme Lord shines like the Self, but not as a separate "this-ness.

According to this principle stated in the *Pratyabhijñā*, because they do not transcend the level of the subject (*pramātṛ*), there is no contraction of consciousness—as there is, for example, in the case of the body or the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*). Therefore, it is entirely logical that they possess omniscience and other such qualities.
And this [is stated] as follows:
"But when difference appears as having a single flavor," as has been demonstrated at length in the *Śrīpratyabhijñākārikāṭīkā*.

Thus, this should be explained with reference to the infinite lords (bhaṭṭāraka) and others who preside over the effects such as emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) while abiding in the state of the Word of Knowledge (*vidyāpada*).

Likewise, for the teachers (*ācārya*) and others engaged in initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth, all mantras— which are of the nature of instruments— seize the power that consists of the reality of its vibration (*spanda-tattva*), and having sustained it as their vitalizing breath (*anuprāṇaka*), they proceed toward the authority for the means of liberation, enjoyment, and so on, together with the mind of the worshipper belonging specifically to those teachers; in that very state, they take on the form of a body consisting of words that signify tranquility.

And for this very reason, being stainless and pure, they dissolve completely and find rest. In this explanation, the phrase "together with the mind of the worshipper" is to be connected with the preceding verse.
And thus, although it pervades the limits of the arising and dissolution of mantras during their manifestation, it is described as being their foundational support (*bhittibhūta*).
*And thus it has been stated that within the Śaiva tradition, which is divided into ten, eighteen, and other such categories, the essence of mantras is precisely the principle of *spanda*.

*Having thus established that the creation conceived as pure—consisting of the forms of Mantras, Mantreśvaras, and so forth—is the very nature of Śiva, [the author] now demonstrates that even that creation conceived as impure, consisting of the forms of Māyā and the rest, is indeed the essential form of Śiva himself; thereby revealing the perspective of the secret teachings of the *Śrīmata* scriptures and others.*
He further suggests:
"Because the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of everything, since it arises from all states of being;
for it attains identity [with them] through the nature of their perception. (VSpk 2.3)
Therefore, in the contemplation of words and their meanings, there is no state that is not Śiva;
for the enjoyer himself always abides everywhere in the form of the enjoyed.
Since the individual soul (*jīva*) is the perceiver, consists of all things, and—like Śiva—possesses the universal form, for that reason, with respect to words as the signifiers and their meanings...
Among the objects of expression and among thoughts consisting of conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) and so forth, there is no state—whether in the beginning, middle, or end—that is not Śiva;
the meaning is that everything is indeed the very nature of Śiva.

And since this is so, the enjoyer alone, whose essence is consciousness (*cidātman*), is the subject who always and eternally exists in the form of the body, blue objects, and so forth, as the object of enjoyment.

Abiding everywhere— in all states such as the various principles (*tattva*) and worlds (*bhuvana*)— perfectly, without deficiency or excess, there is no so-called object of enjoyment that is distinct from the enjoyer. By beginning with "the individual soul" (*jīva*) and concluding with "Śiva," it is shown that there is no real difference whatsoever between the individual soul and Śiva.

He teaches by way of a specific method that, in none of the states of the body and so forth, should a sense of incompleteness be conceived; rather, [the body] is of the very nature of Śiva, who is a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*).
As it has been said: "Those who perceive even the body as consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*) and as being the form of Śiva, and who worship it..."
"They succeed; having become thus absorbed, they see [the object] as if it were a jar or the like, and they also worship it. There is no dispute on this point, as stated in the *Śrīpratyabhijñāṭīkā*.
Bhaṭṭa Śrīvāmana has also said:

"Since consciousness, having taken an object, does not [perceive it] by way of its own intrinsic nature, therefore everything is known; thus one should become composed of consciousness. // VSpkC_2.3-4:5 // Thus. VSpkC_2.3-4:6

* Why is the individual soul (*jīva*) said to consist of everything? The reason here is that it is the source of the emergence of all existents, being their cause of origin; furthermore, this designation emphasizes its status as the substratum (*apādāna*). Since you are the cause of the entire collection of distinctions consisting of the knower, the cognition, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, your abiding state (*vihāra*) here serves as that cause. Because [these distinctions] cease to manifest in you at any time, that [distinction] disappears; therefore, by this principle, the path [of duality] is never again perceived by anyone in the world.
Thus, according to the principle stated in the *Śrījñānagarbha-stotra*, since the world exists only when consciousness has expanded, the soul is the source from which all things arise;
and since the universe emerges from the soul alone, it follows that this [soul] consists of everything and is the power of the universe (*viśvaśakti*).
This has been established in the commentary on the second aphorism.
* He states another reason for the state of being "consisting of all" (*sarvamayatva*) with the half-verse beginning with "in the cognition of that" (*tatsaṃvedane*).

(VSpkC 2.3–4:11) Because one realizes identity (*tādātmya*) with that which is the cognition—the manifestation—of all that [appears], such as blue, pleasure, and so forth; that is, because the state of consisting of all is perceived through that very form or nature.
(VSpkC 2.3–4:12) Thus, by these two verses, the secret practices (*rahasyacaryā*) are presented, which are constructed as the means for uprooting the tree of all dualistic distinctions.

By means of the first and last sūtras, the discourse on the instruction of knowledge [is presented]; by the sūtra beginning with "jāgrat" (the waking state), the supreme reality of the Trika (ṣaḍardha) is [shown];

and by the phrase "having ascended that," it is suggested that this is the essence of all forms of worship, and so forth. Thus, through the *spandatattva* alone, all instructions for the universe have been embraced.
Or rather, for one who possesses the realization that "liberation is precisely the essence of this practice," and who perceives the entire world as a play—
constantly seeing thus and remaining disciplined, he is liberated while living; of this there is no doubt.
The word "or" (*vā*), by suggesting an alternative to the previously mentioned mode of meditative absorption characterized by closing the eyes, implies the extreme rarity of this attainment.

This is the meaning: such a realization is difficult to obtain; it occurs only for someone in their final birth, who perceives the entire world as a play, creating and withdrawing it through the opening and closing of his own consciousness.

"Those who, fixing their minds on me, worship me with constant discipline"—by abiding in this state, the great yogi is perpetually permeated by it; even while living and possessing breath and other vital functions, he has all bonds completely consumed by the fire of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*). Upon the fall of the body, he is indeed Śiva himself. Even if living, such a one is liberated and is not bound in any way whatsoever.

By the phrase "there is no doubt," he suggests this: liberation [is attained] through initiation and so forth by means of conviction in the Guru; however, from such knowledge or right conduct, it occurs precisely through one's own conviction.
(VSpkC 2.5:4) He states in two verses that this very Great Attainment (*mahāsamāpatti*) is the cause for the practitioners, teachers, and others to attain their desired goal:
"This alone is the arising of that object of meditation within the mind of the meditator. (VSpkC 2.5:5)
It is the meditative attainment of identity with that [deity] for the practitioner who so desires.
This alone is the attainment of immortality; this alone is the grasping of the Self;
and this is the initiation into Nirvāṇa, which bestows the true being of Śiva.
Regarding that which is proclaimed—"having become Śiva here, one should worship Śiva"—it resides in the consciousness of the meditator's mind.

The phrase "of that" refers to the arising or manifestation of this very [state]—whether it be the object of meditation whose nature has been established as Śiva, or some other specific mantra-deity who is the cause of various accomplishments—for the practitioner, meditator, teacher, or whoever else [is concerned]. It is not that there is no state which is Śiva; rather, this is what has been taught.

"Therefore, in the contemplations of word and meaning, there is no state that is not Śiva. (VSpkC 2.6–7). Thus, the realization of identity (*tadātmatā-samāpatti*)—which has been established as such—is the immersion into oneness with Śiva; it is not the perception of a form distinct from the five faces and so forth, nor is the realization of identity achieved through mere conceptual certainty alone. Rather, it belongs to one who, desiring it, is mounted upon the reflective awareness of the will, which consists of the non-conceptual "I-ness" (*ahantā*) of the universe and the oneness with Śiva.

This is what is meant: "I alone am Śiva, the mass of consciousness and bliss whose body is the universe, because I have realized identity with Him through the nature of that very awareness. For one whose such resolve bears fruit by becoming free of all conceptual construction (*avikalpaśeṣībhūta*), why indeed would the object of meditation, the mantra, the deity, and so forth, not manifest before them? For everything is attached to this manifestation of non-duality.
As it has been said by our supreme preceptor:
"O Lord, when the entire interior of the world is directly composed of You, what [place] is not a field for those possessed of devotion? Where would a mantra not be effective for them? (VSpkC 2.6–7)
Thus [it is said].

And this very meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) is the acquisition of the nectar (*amṛta*) whose nature is supreme non-duality; for even if practitioners were to acquire some other kind of nectar that merely bestows firmness upon the body for a limited time, death would inevitably still be encountered by them—such is the intended meaning of the word "only" (*eva*).
Thus, with this very intention throughout, in the section on the attainment of the nectar (*amṛta*) through the gross perspective in the *Śrīsvacchanda*, [the text] concludes by stating:
"And by means of the yoga of nectar alone, there can be no victory over time and death.
Having thus concluded, the method for attaining that [nectar] in its ultimate sense [is presented].
"Alternatively, one who abides in the supreme reality is not afflicted at any time," and so forth;
thus,
one should contemplate everything as consisting of the power (*śakti*) of Śiva.
Thus, by means of the middle [path]:
"He who always maintains this contemplation is liberated even while living;
he who constantly contemplates Śiva—time cannot affect him."
The yogi, by means of the yoga of freedom (*svacchanda-yoga*) which moves with a free course, being joined to the state of freedom, shall attain equality with freedom. Being truly free,
he shall always move about in freedom.

Thus, with this spontaneous composition, [the teaching] was subsequently imparted with praise. This very grasping of the self is what is called "knowledge"—that which is stated as "the self is to be known. In that regard, knowledge of the self is precisely this recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the self as having the nature of Śiva, who is omniscient, the agent of all, and independent; it is not, however, [as some claim]: *Vimalaprabhā*, 2.6–7:12. *This very grasping of the self is what is called "knowledge"—that which is stated as "the self is to be known. In that regard, knowledge of the self is precisely this recognition of the self as having the nature of Śiva, who is omniscient, the agent of all, and independent;
it is not [the mere negation of the ego].*
"Verily, this all is the Person alone"—
thus it is declared by those who know the Upanishads.
All those who worship the Self do not go to the supreme state.
Because of this traditional teaching (*āmnāya*):

"Likewise, at the time of initiation, for the purpose of unification (*yojanikā*) and so forth, this very [process] is the grace bestowed upon the self of the disciple. The meaning is that the teacher who knows this very state of absorption (*samāpatti*), by uniting the self of the disciple with Śiva, becomes a true teacher.

This is the initiation of liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*), established through one's own direct realization, which bestows the ultimate nature—the state of being Śiva—upon the 'spiritual son' (*putraka*) and others."
As it has been said:
"For one who knows thus according to reality, initiation—which bestows nirvāṇa—becomes certain, even without the oblations of sesame seeds and clarified butter. (VSpkC 2.6–7:18)
Thus [ends the section].

Regarding the phrase "the initiation of the Hotṛ priest is also indeed initiation" (VSpkC 2.6–7): the venerable and most eminent Great Guru did not employ the restrictive particle *eva* here with the intention that no one should have any lack of confidence in this matter. May there be auspiciousness! [End of] Spandakārikā.
The third is the outflow (niḥṣyanda):

just as the Creator, when requested according to one's desire, brings about for embodied beings the rising of the moon and sun so that they may attain the objects situated in their hearts while awake.

Likewise, because he never transgresses his affection for desired objects even in dreams, he who stands in the center must necessarily manifest them most clearly. (VSpk 3.2) He is the Sustainer (*dhātṛ*) because he holds everything within himself; he is Śaṅkara by nature, just as for one who is awake—that is, for one whose own sovereignty is manifested during the waking state.

Requested by the will of the embodied yogi— whose knowledge residing in the physical body has become manifest— and gratified by the power of the inward-turned self-reflection (*vimarśa*), [the Lord] accomplishes within the heart and mind the purposes of the objects situated there, such as the movement of the vibration and intuition of the *bindu*, *nāda*, and other [phonemic energies], preceded by the knowledge of them.

How so? Having brought about the emergence of the moon and the sun—the powers of knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*)—that which is illuminated by the power of knowledge is indeed manifested by each respective power of action. (VSpkC 3.1–2:2) The Supreme Lord, having entered the body of the yogin, effects the penetration of various [levels of] piercing (*vedha*) and so forth, through the process of expanding the rays of light—both those on the right and others—which have as their essence the pervasion of the powers of knowledge and action. This expansion is brought about by the method of firm grounding in the root, which consists of the dawning intuition (*pratibhā*) of immersion (*samāveśa*). (VSpkC 3.1–2:3)
And just as it is so, thus:
when sleep has not yet arrived and the external object of perception has perished,
that state accessible to the mind shines forth as the supreme goddess.
Thus:
"Having meditated upon one's power as both robust and weak within the twelvefold field,
and having entered the heart while meditating, one attains mastery over dreams."

Thus, according to the established tradition, for one who does not transcend the eternal *praṇaya* by means of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the power of consciousness— the source of emission consisting of both [the powers] intent upon vomiting and swallowing— being solely devoted to the prayer to the Lord and established in yogic sleep, the Creator, abiding in the center of the *suṣumnā* channel, bestows even in dreams only those desired things, such as the absorptions (*samāveśa*) of the individual (*āṇava*), the empowered (*śākta*), and the supreme (*śāmbhava*).
Furthermore, for this yogi whose mirror of the intellect has been polished by the practice of immersion (*samāveśa*), all objects he desires to know necessarily become manifest;
the meaning is that no delusion occurs for him even in the states of dream or deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
(The state of deep sleep is indicated here by the mention of "dream.")

In this manifestation of the desired object, this very [devotion] is the cause; for by the grace (*prasāda*)—characterized by the subsiding of the turbidity of *māyā* and attainable through the worship consisting of the inward-turning contemplation of one's own nature—the Lord does not transgress the petitioner’s request. Indeed, the Supreme Lord, whose essence is consciousness, accomplishes whatever is sought when He is petitioned through the sequence of service appropriate to the inward-turned state.

The phrase "thus for one who is awake" (evaṃ jāgrataḥ) should be explained through a double entendre (*śleṣokti*) as referring both to one who is vigilant regarding the supreme reality (*paratattva*) and to one who is situated in the state of waking (*jāgarāvasthā*).
Furthermore, he states that if one is not thus attentive, then one does not possess the status of a yogin:
"Otherwise, however, creation would be independent, because it would possess that [very same] nature."
Just as for an ordinary person, [this occurs] constantly in both the states of waking and dreaming.

(VSpk 3.3) If the Sustainer is not constantly propitiated through reasoned logic, then, in the absence of abiding in one's own true nature, for this yogin as well—as for an ordinary person—there will constantly, day after day, be the manifestation and determination of common and uncommon objects in both waking and dreaming. His essential nature [will remain characterized by these].
The meaning is that if the creation belonging to the Supreme Lord were independent, like that of worldly beings, it would cause even the yogin to fall into the pit of saṃsāra.
As it has been said:
"The activity of beings is divine" (VSpkC 3.3:2).
"Because of having that as its nature" (VSpkC 3.3:3) means that, in the manifestation of states such as dreaming and waking, [it proceeds] from the independent nature of the Lord's creation.

Having thus established the means for crushing dreams and deep sleep for the sake of one's own awakening, he now describes the means for entering the reality of Spanda (vibration) for the fully awakened one, supported by examples and reasoning, and instructs that even the cognition of the object sought occurs in this manner:
"For just as an object, though seen with an attentive mind, remains indistinct..."
Cultivated through the exertion of its own power, it shines forth even more clearly.
Thus, having mastered that power exactly as it exists— by what means, where, and in what manner according to the ultimate truth— it proceeds forth before long.
(*The word "hi" has the sense of the particle "kila.")

Just as an object, though perceived indistinctly due to defects such as distance even when the mind is attentive, appears not only clearly but even more clearly when it is intensely contemplated and repeatedly observed through the nature of direct perception by means of the exertion of its own power— so too does that power whose essence is the reality of Spanda, by which [the Self] exists in the Supreme Reality consisting of the mass of bliss within the Self of Śaṅkara.

"In its own nature, just as it is"—meaning it exists through non-dual pervasion (*abhedavyāpti*)—so too does that agent [of manifestation] proceed; "just so" means that by means of the exertion of one's own power, through the effort of cultivating the state of being of one essence with that [reality] directed inwardly, it is brought forth and becomes manifest very quickly with extreme clarity.
How? By having first overwhelmed the level of the limited subject consisting of the imagined body and so forth belonging to the worshipper, and having caused it to be submerged within one's own self.

And for the practitioner-yogin who, having ascended by means of the power whose nature is vibration, repeatedly rouses the plane of the subject consisting of the imagined body and intellect, whatever is desired to be known— such as a treasure— and in whatever place, by whatever material such as gold, in what ultimate sense,
and with what configuration it exists, that very thing manifests immediately.
He states that even the power of the agent and so forth arises by the force of this very [consciousness]:
"Since even a weak person, having taken hold of it, proceeds to action;
and likewise, one who is extremely hungry might suppress his hunger. (VSpk 3.6)

Just as one whose vital essence (*dhātu*) is exhausted, yet who is like a sage, having seized power characterized by vibration (*spanda*), repeatedly energizes the plane of the subject that is the vital breath (*prāṇa-pramātṛ-bhūmi*) through the force of the penetration of vibration (*spanda-samāveśa*), and thus engages in necessary tasks and actions; the meaning is that even an impossible object is accomplished solely by seizing that power of vibration.
Likewise, even one who is extremely hungry pacifies hunger, thirst, and the like through the force of that [state].

For there is no subjugation by the pairs of opposites for one who has entered the plane of the mass of consciousness (*cidghana*); such subjugation belongs only to the plane of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, because that [subjugation] depends upon them, and because those [vital breaths] are here submerged in this plane of consciousness.
Since this collection of accomplishments arises from this [plane] according to the sequence of reasoning stated in the aforementioned aphorisms, therefore—
Just as omniscience and other qualities exist when the body is presided over by this [power],
so too will it be everywhere through the presiding over one's own self.

(VSpk 3.7) [When the body] is presided over— that is, pervaded— by this Spanda-principle, which is one's own essential nature, then, just as [the powers] take the form of the instruments for experiencing objects appropriate to that particular state, etc.,...
Just as the qualities of omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth manifest for an embodied being, so too, if this [individual]— like the withdrawal of a tortoise’s limbs—
effects a grounding within its own imperishable self, which is of the nature of consciousness (cidrūpa), either by withdrawing everything or through the method of great expansion,

and establishes a state of immersion (*samāveśa*) in that very self which has been recognized and re-recognized through the aforementioned higher knowledges (*abhijñāna*), then [the powers manifest] everywhere.
"Thus, from Śiva down to the earth," [it means] he will become one whose nature consists of being Śaṅkara, as well as appropriate omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth.
[Regarding the statement] "even this [attainment] is by his grace," he says:
"Lassitude is that which withers the body, and its course arises from ignorance."

If that [state] were destroyed by its own unfolding, how could it be causeless? [It is the locus of all afflictions; therefore, the exhaustion in the body—which, for the person who identifies with the body, is the loss of joy—is a plunderer. By seizing the wealth of supreme consciousness, it bestows the poverty of limitation. And from that exhaustion, due to ignorance...]
Because of the non-recognition (*apratyabhijñāna*) of one's own true nature, which is a mass of consciousness and bliss (*cidānandaghana*), there is the cycle of birth, emergence, and persistence.

If that ignorance—which will be shown to consist of the nature of [the Lord's] unfolding (*unmeṣa*)—is destroyed or cut away, then how could this exhaustion (*glāni*) exist? The meaning is that it would not exist, because its cause, the self of ignorance, is absent.
And in the absence of exhaustion, even the states of affliction such as disease, which are inevitable in the body, [occur] for the yogi in whatever manner [they may].
Just as gold being intensely heated shines forth its own true nature once all impurities have been removed,
so too, even while remaining in the body, the constant absence of weariness is the supernatural power (*vibhūti*) of the supreme yogin.
As it was said by the supreme yoginī Madālasā while employing young children [as her instruments]:
"Do not fall into delusion regarding this body of yours, which is like a garment that must be cast off when it begins to decay.
This body has been bound to you as a garment by auspicious and inauspicious karmas, and by pride and other such afflictions.

By this [verse], it is also demonstrated through a particular turn of phrase that for a yogin who desires limited supernatural powers (*mitasiddhi*) and pierces the body through the relish of practicing immersion (*samāveśa*), there occurs victory over diseases such as wrinkles and grey hair.
Now, in response to the inquiry as to what the nature of this "unmesha" (opening) is and by what means it is to be attained, he says:
"That which, for one intent upon a single thought, results in the arising of another, should be known as unmesha;
one should perceive it for oneself. (VSpk 3.9)
"When mental objects (*bhāva*) are abandoned and consciousness (*citta*) has ceased, it does not go toward another object;
at that time, through the state of being in the midst of that, the supreme cultivation (*atibhāvanā*) blossoms.
According to this principle, for one who is intent upon some particular form of contemplation whose nature consists of a stillness focused on a specific object of support (*ālambana*),...

For the yogin who has become one-pointed, because of the expansion of consciousness shining forth from the excellence of that very one-pointedness, there occurs—due to the closing of the objective support—a sudden swallowing up of the entire stream of thought. From the *spanda-tattva*, which is of the nature of the non-differentiation of fire and moon, there arises another, indeed a distinct, supramundane effulgence consisting of the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*). That should be understood and sought as "unfolding" (*unmeṣa*), precisely because it causes the unfolding of that wonder.

In this very way, it can be known by the yogi; and because it is "itself" (*svayam*), being devoid of the objective status of "this-ness" (*idantā*), one should perceive it within oneself by means of the very "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃtā*) through an attentiveness that is unconditioned effort.
One should recognize it through its unique nature as wonder (*camatkāra*).

Others [hold] that when one who is engaged in a thought concerning the investigation of an object, etc., there occurs the sudden emergence of another thought, that which pervades both thoughts is "unfolding" (*unmeṣa*).

Now, he instructs that even those various supernatural powers (*siddhis*) which are accomplished through the effort of practitioners of limited yoga—powers that arise merely from the cultivation of the upward movement (*unmeṣa*)—must be regarded as things to be abandoned by the supreme yogin:

"From this [state], the drop (*bindu*), from this the sound (*nāda*), from this the form (*rūpa*), and from this the taste (*rasa*) proceed very quickly for the embodied being as causes of agitation. (VSpk 3.10)

From this unfolding (*unmeṣa*), which is being perceived while the yogin’s sense of "I" regarding the gross and subtle bodies and so forth does not dissolve, there arises in a very short time at the center of the eyebrows and other locations: the *bindu*, whose nature is the light of the star; the *nāda*, whose nature is the light common to all objects of knowledge; the form of the *anāhata* resonance, which is the sound that is undifferentiated from all expressive words; the light which is illumination even in darkness; and the extraordinary taste at the tip of the tongue.
The flavors (āsvādas) exist as obstacles to the attainment of the principle of vibration (spandatattva) by means of their agitation, while providing a sense of satisfaction for the time being.
As they say:
"These are hindrances in meditative absorption (samādhi), but accomplishments (siddhis) in the state of emergence (vyutthāna)."
Thus [it is said].

(VSpkC_3.10:2) It has been stated that even for a yogin who is intent on observing the unfolding [of consciousness] (*unmeṣa*), yet who still identifies the body as the self, the *bindu*, *nāda*, and so forth become causes of agitation.

(VSpkC_3.10:3) Now, he says that one immerses the state of being a limited subject (*dehapramātṛtā*) into this very nature which consists of the unfolding, and thereby attains the supreme subjectivity (*parapramātṛtā*) which takes that [nature] as its form. (VSpkC_3.10:4)
When it remains pervading all objects as if out of a desire to see them, then what is the use of much speaking? One will understand by oneself alone.

(VSpk 3.11) [Just as at the moment of the desire to see (*didṛkṣā*), which is non-conceptual in nature like that of the *paśyantī* stage, the object desired to be seen flashes forth with its internal distinctions.]

In the same way, having pervaded all objects— from the earth up to Śiva— contained within the cosmological sequence described in the *Svacchanda* and other scriptures, one remains when, like Sadāśiva, one covers everything with the realization "I am all" through the internal integration of non-dual reflective awareness (*abhedavimarśa*), preceded by the synthesis of one's own conceptualizations, and does not waver from this meditative absorption (*samāpatti*). At that time, there arises the wonder of immersion into the state of the Great Subject (*mahāpramātṛtā*), which, by unifying all objects of knowledge, devours those very objects as they emerge.
That fruit he will realize by himself; his own consciousness alone will experience it. What is the use of much exposition on this matter?

Having asserted that "its perception is constant," it was subsequently established that for one who practices the collection of means, the state of being constantly permeated by the reality of *spanda* arises for the well-awakened one, because [that state] is inseparable from the infinite objects of knowledge.
Recalling this within the heart of the disciple, he speaks by way of a summary concerning the method of entry:
"Always remaining awakened, having perceived the objective field through knowledge, one should unify everything in one; thereby, one is not oppressed by anything else. (VSpk 3.12)

Always awakened, one should remain in all states—waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and consciousness, as well as at their beginning, middle, and end—possessing the divine vision that rests upon the unveiled reality of *spanda*. One should thus attain the state of perfect awakening.
How so? By means of knowledge, having perceived every object within its field of experience—the blue, pleasure, and so forth—through outward-directed manifestation.
Therefore, among the thoughts of words and their meanings, there is no state that is not Śiva.

Having reflected in this manner as established above, one should project everything onto the single creator, the essential nature which is Śaṅkara himself; one should know [all things] through their non-difference from Him in both the states of closing and opening [the eyes]. The meaning is that, through the firmness gained by supporting oneself on the prior and posterior limits, one should perceive even the intermediate state as nothing other than the solidification of the essence of consciousness (*cidrasa*).
And thus, it is not sublated by any other distinct entity, because [all things] are accepted as being one's own self (*svātman*).
As it has been said by the venerable author of the *Pratyabhijñā*:
"O Lord, he who perceives this entire egg-born universe as your body, without conceptual construction (*avikalpa*),"

"When the world is completely filled with one's own self, how can there be fear for this eternally blissful one? (VSpkC 3.12). Regarding what was stated there—that he is not oppressed by another—one might raise the doubt: "Who is this oppressor and who is the oppressed, since the universe has been declared to be of the very nature of Śiva? In response to this, [the text addresses] the fetters (*pāśa*) and the bound soul (*paśu*).
In order to determine its essential nature, he says:

"Having become one whose power is eclipsed by *kalā*, that [Self] who has fallen into the state of being an object of enjoyment for the group of powers arising from the mass of sounds is known as a *paśu* (bound soul). (VSpk 3.13)
In this context, that very nature of Śiva which has been described as having the essence of light—
this Lord, established as the cause of the universe,
performs creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace.

Thus, according to the perspective of the venerable *Svacchanda-śāstra*, He who is eternally embraced by His own power, who performs the fivefold cosmic acts, and who is autonomous, is proclaimed in the scriptures by such names as Spanda, Lalita, Īśvara, and others. (VSpkC 3.13:2) His very power of autonomy (*svātantrya-śakti*), which is eternal, consists of the nature of the perfect I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*). It is designated in various places by countless names such as Parā, Matsyodarī, Mahāsattā, Sphurattā, Ūrmī, Sārā, Hṛdayā, Bhairavī, Devī, Śikhā, and so forth. (VSpkC 3.13:3)

The Supreme Speech (*parā vāk*) is the very fullness of I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*), which, having embraced the venerable letters from *a* to *kṣa* through their union with the unsurpassed power of the Unstruck (*anāhata*), consists of the expansion of the six paths in the form of the infinite signified and signifying. Having internalized and encompassed the entire wheel of powers (*śakticakra*) and the entire succession of creations, dissolutions, and so forth, it is of the nature of non-sequential awareness (*akramavimarśa*). It consists of the eternally arisen, unutterable Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*), and is the life-force of all living beings.

This very [power] of the Lord vibrates, manifesting within itself, as it were, the state of movement of such a manifold variety of the universe; thus, because it follows this meaning, it is here called "spanda" (vibration). And so, while the Lord desires to effect the manifestation—even part by part—of His own Self upon the wall of His own nature through the play of concealing His true form, that [power], though indeed one and non-different, remains as such.

His power of self-reflective awareness (vimarśa-śakti), having attained the state of will (icchā) and abiding as knowledge and action, becomes twofold through the distinction between the seed-syllables (bīja) and matrices (yoni) consisting of the reflective awareness of Śiva and Śakti; it then manifests ninefold through the division of the consonant groups and fiftyfold through the division of their phonetic components. Thus manifesting through forms that are the essence of his awareness—namely, the Aghora, Ghora, and Ghoratara deities of consciousness—it effects the fivefold activity of the Lord.
It proceeds as it is stated in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*:
"That power of the Creator of the world which is said to be inherent (*samavāyinī*)."
That goddess assumes the nature of desire for him who wishes to create.
Listen now to how she, though being one, attains multiplicity;
it should be known with absolute certainty that "it is exactly thus, and not otherwise."
When she makes known [the intention] here in this world, she is called the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*);
when she is oriented toward action, thinking "let all this be so," she is then said to be the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) as she brings that object into being.

Thus, although she is of two forms, the Sovereign Lady attains infinity through further divisions by virtue of the limiting adjuncts of objects, like a wish-fulfilling gem. Therein, having first entered into the state of absorption, she differentiates herself into the nature of the Mothers.

The Mālinī is twofold, ninefold, and indeed fiftyfold. It is twofold due to the distinction between the nature of seed-syllables (*bīja*) and matrices (*yoni*); the vowels are considered to be the seeds. The consonants beginning with *ka* are remembered as the matrices; they are ninefold according to the division of the classes (*varga*).
Blazing with fifty rays through the differentiation of distinct colors,
Śiva is here designated as the seed (*bīja*) and Śakti as the womb (*yoni*).
It should be known that the eight groups (*varga*) follow in sequence, beginning with Aghora.
That very [group] is the eightfold [set] beginning with Māheśvarī through the differentiation of powers; and,
O fair-faced one, it is further divided into five hundred varieties,
conceived by the Supreme Lord as the designators of the Rudras.
And in that very same way, [it proceeds] from the sequence of those powers and their enumerations;
thus it begins, and so forth. Likewise:
Those others, however, who are even more terrible (*ghoratara*), embrace the Rudra-entities (*rudrāṇu*) and cause them to fall lower and lower, deeply attached to sense objects;
they produce an attachment to the fruits of mixed karma, as before.
The Aghorā Śiva-śaktis, which obstruct the path to liberation, are known as the Ghorā-parāparas;
like before, they bestow upon the multitude of living beings the fruit of the abode of Śiva.
Those who know the truth have declared these to be the Parā [śaktis].
Thus: VSpkC_3.13:22–23.

In this way, that very group of nine classes (*varganavaka*) which has arisen from the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*), consisting of the groups of deities beginning with Brāhmī together with Śiva—when it becomes an object of enjoyment for those who perceive it, that very nature whose essence is Śaṅkara is traditionally known as the bound soul (*paśu*) in the Āgamas; so it is stated therein.

Now, to pacify the doubt as to how the Enjoyer, Maheśvara, could have reached this state, he states the reason by means of a qualification: "one whose power has been eclipsed by *kalā*. *Kalā* is the power of *māyā*, so called because it "measures" (*kalayati*), casts out, or delimits [the soul] through limitation. The meaning is that his majesty has been eclipsed by that [power]; he remains with his sovereignty concealed by his own *māyā*.

And yet, because his power—consisting of the reinforcement of limited agency (*kiṃcitkartṛtva*) through the principle of *kalā*—is characterized by that [power], he has his glory eclipsed and his attributes such as fullness and agency obscured by the "mantle" consisting of *kalā*, *vidyā*, *kāla*, *niyati*, and *rāga*.
[Objection: "Let this be so; but how has he come to be an object of enjoyment for the group of powers? [Reply: To this, the answer is precisely this:
by means of the *kalās*—namely, Brāhmī and the others, who preside over the groups beginning with the letter 'A' and who act as the presiding deities over those venerable phonemes.

And because my power has been eclipsed by the "parts" (kalās)—the letters beginning with *a* which take the form of the deities described in the *Śrīmālinīvijaya*—I am contracted, incomplete, and distressed by the penetration of gross and subtle sounds through a multitude of various conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions such as "I shall do this," "I shall take this," or "I shall abandon this. As if being led toward states such as joy and sorrow, I do not attain stability in my own true nature even for a moment; therefore, he [is as follows].

The bound soul (*paśu*), as previously described, is said to be consumed by the group of powers (*kalā*). By means of *kalā*, which consists of non-recognition (*akhyāti*), his power is eclipsed; he appears as if contracted, though not in reality. His true nature, which is essentially Śiva, has not departed anywhere. For in the absence of that [power], he himself would not manifest.

Thus, the meaning is that his power is eclipsed by the contracted categories (*kalā*) appearing in such a way—namely, by limited sounds and cognitions—and consequently, he is incapable of reflecting upon his own self as being of such a [divine] nature.
Now, he analyzes how the bound soul (*paśu*)—whose power of vision is contracted—is both that which is to be bound and that which binds:
"The depletion of the nectar of the Supreme (*parāmṛta*) for him arises from the emergence of [dualistic] cognitions (*pratyaya*).
Through that, he attains a state of lack of autonomy (*asvatantratā*), and that [depletion] has as its object only the subtle elements (*tanmātra*). (VSpk 3.14)

The emergence—that is, the birth tainted by destruction—of those perceptions of that animal, which consist of worldly and scriptural conceptualizations and are the arising of various cognitions of objects perfumed by them; that is the loss, the submergence, of the supreme nectar-essence, the mass of consciousness, the outpouring of bliss. (VSpkC 3.14:1)

When various cognitions (*pratyaya*) with distinct objects have arisen, the ground of consciousness (*cidbhūmi*), although present, appears as if non-existent because it is not being reflected upon; for this reason, it has been said thus.
And by the arising of those cognitions, this [consciousness] falls into a state of dependence and becomes subject to their power.
As it is stated in the venerable *Śivasūtras*: "Knowledge is bondage."
The venerable sage Vyāsa also said: "In childhood, one consists of mother and father. The venerable Ālasā also said:
"Sometimes as 'father,' sometimes as 'son,' sometimes as 'mother,' and sometimes as 'beloved.'"
"Nothing is 'mine,' nor is anything 'not mine'; do not speak in many ways to this deluded assembly.
(VSpkC 3.14:7) Thus [it is said].

(VSpkC 3.14:8) The meaning is that its object consists of distinct things to be known—that is, its range is such that its conditions arise as the mere elements (*tanmātra*), with functions characterized by the distinctions of intense, non-intense, and common. (VSpkC 3.14:9)

By this he says the following: as long as there is this manifestation of divided objects of experience, one is indeed bound; however, when—through the reasoning of the aforementioned instruction—one realizes with unwavering conviction that everything is composed of the Self alone, then one is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). As it has been said: "He whose consciousness... and so forth.

And thus, there is no discrepancy whatsoever between what was stated previously—"Therefore, in the contemplations of word and meaning, there is no state that is not Śiva"—and the statement: "The emergence of cognition in him is the depletion of the nectar of supreme immortality. Now, one might raise the objection: "If even the emergence of cognition is for him a depletion of the nectar of supreme immortality, then how can it be said that he has become the object of enjoyment for the group of powers? To dispel this doubt, [the author] says: VSpkC_3.14:13]
And its powers for veiling its own nature are perpetually active, because the arising of cognition does not occur without the interpenetration of words. [Note:
The particle *ca* indicates a doubt and introduces another object of knowledge (*prameya*) as a means to resolve that doubt.]
When this sacrificial victim— whose own form is that of Śiva— does not correctly reflect upon his nature, even though that nature manifests as the foundational substrate for its concealment,

the powers whose forms have been explained arise constantly on account of that [non-reflection]. For as long as the recognition of his own essential nature, which consists of the essence of the supreme nectar, has not occurred for him, these powers continue to exert themselves toward the concealment of his own true nature.

Since the flow of his conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions arising from conditions does not occur without being permeated by sound— whether through the subtle internal coloring by sound in such forms as "I know this," or through association with gross verbal expression— even in animals there exists a non-conventional, quasi-indicative form within themselves, resembling the pointing of a finger toward one's own self.

There certainly exists a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that is not [merely] verbal; otherwise, a child’s initial grasping of linguistic conventions would be impossible, because it would be devoid of the reflective awareness consisting of internal inclusion and exclusion (*antarūhāpoha*).
However, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which consists of the interpenetration of gross words, is established by everyone’s own experience.

Concluding the meaning stated in these three verses, [the author] establishes that the object of knowledge is necessarily non-different from the reality of the universal vibration (*sāmānyaspandatattva*).
Following what was stated previously, he characterizes bondage and liberation as consisting of the non-recognition and recognition, respectively, of that [power]:

"This very power, whose nature is action, belonging to Śiva and residing within the bound soul (paśu), is the binder when it remains on its own path; when known, it brings about accomplishment. (VSpk 3.16)

Because it has been determined by these three verses, this [power]—manifesting in the form that extends to the objects of knowledge (*prameya*)—is indeed the Supreme Goddess (*Parābhaṭṭārikā*), whose nature is the *Spanda* principle and who belongs to Śiva, the conscious Self whose own nature is light. Since she is the cause of the manifestation of the world's manifold variety, she is the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). According to the perspective previously established, while residing in one who has assumed the state of a bound soul (*paśu*), she takes on the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*).

When she sprinkles this [Self] with the droplet of egoity (*ahaṃtā*) by means of its nature as an agent, and thus fails to recognize it in its true form— because that [egoity] obscures one's own essential nature and because it is the cause of the afflictions of grasping and rejecting— it becomes the binder. However, when there is the path to one's own auspicious (*śiva*) nature...
"For one who has entered the state of power (*śakti*), there is meditation without differentiation;
at that time, he becomes identical with Śiva—this is here called the 'mouth of Śiva'.

According to the principle stated by the venerable Vijñānabhaṭṭāraka in this verse, the means of attainment is the Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*); through identity with her, this [power] is known as the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).

Or when the yogi perceives that all objects of knowledge— which constitute a part of his own self whose nature is Śiva— even amidst the flow of both conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions, then this [perception] brings him to the supreme accomplishment (*siddhi*) consisting of supreme bliss.
[VSpkC 3.16:3] By means of the emergence of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), which reside within the mind, the ego, and the intellect...
Constrained by the city of eight, it experiences that which arises from the resulting cognitions.
Under the power of another, it experiences enjoyment; because of that state, it wanders through saṃsāra.
Therefore, we shall explain the cause for the dissolution of this saṃsāra.
(VSpk 3.18) [It experiences enjoyment arising from the *puryaṣṭaka*. (VSpkC 3.17–18:1)]

Precisely because the cognition of pleasure and so forth arises within the causal conditions (*pratyaya*), for that very reason this bound soul (*paśu*) is dependent on others due to the arising of those conditions;
being drawn along at every step by the goddesses beginning with Brāhmī through the process of the permeation of sound, he is not independent like one who is perfectly awakened.
By the very existence of that "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*), his diverse latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are repeatedly awakened, and thus he wanders in transmigratory existence.

Having acquired bodies that serve as the substrates for various enjoyments appropriate to those [states], it grasps and then abandons them. Since this is so, we shall immediately hereafter explain the cause— the correct and easy means— for that supreme dissolution of its transmigratory existence which is constricted by the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*), a dissolution consisting in the eradication of the impurity whose nature is that eightfold city.

We speak thus; in this treatise, we have ourselves established it accordingly. The use of the present tense is justified by the rule: "In proximity to the present, one may use the present tense as if it were current.
Thus ends the application of the present tense.
Demonstrating this, he concludes the meaning stated in the first sūtra:

"But when [the mind] is firmly established in one place, then by restraining its dissolution and emergence, it attains the state of the enjoyer; thereafter, it becomes the Lord of the Wheel. (VSpk 3.19)

Furthermore, when this [practitioner], having thoroughly cultivated the methods of instruction for immersion into the supreme reality (*paratattva*), becomes firmly established, perfectly immovable, and fully absorbed in the single essence of the *spanda* principle— the self consisting of perfect *ahantā*— he then, by means of that very [immersion], governs the dissolution and emergence of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the subtle body) mentioned in the preceding sūtra, and through it, the dissolution and emergence of the entire universe, by means of its closing and opening.

According to the perspective established by the first aphorism, by performing both dissolution and emanation from the single essential nature of Śiva, one attains the state of the enjoyer; and by swallowing the entirety of objects of enjoyment—from the earth up to Śiva—one should, through the process of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), take hold of the very reality that is supreme subjectivity.
Consequently, one becomes the Lord (*īśvara*), the sovereign over the wheel of powers (*śakticakra*), which is the collection of one's own rays, as determined in the first aphorism.
That is to say, by means of this very body, one indeed attains the state of Maheśvara.

Thus, demonstrating the encapsulation of the great purpose (*mahārtha*) between the introduction and the conclusion, the venerable teacher Vasugupta reveals that this scripture stands at the pinnacle of all the Upaniṣads of Śaṅkara, owing to its essential core. May there be auspiciousness!
The *Spandakārikā*, the fourth outflow:
a boat for crossing the unfathomable ocean of doubt.

I pay homage to that wondrous speech of the Guru, which possesses marvelous meanings and words; for, according to the established principle that "the blessed Śaiva Speech, which is not common to the ignorant, is here called the mouth of the Guru," she takes the form of the Teacher because she is the cause for attaining the abode of Śiva. Furthermore, by encompassing the levels of *paśyantī* and the rest, she is the Great Speech (*mahatī bhāratī*), the supreme Word (*parā vāk*), as well as the Guru, the Teacher.
I bow to— that is, I enter into as the most supreme— the wondrous speech that is related [to me] and instructive, which consists of a super-mundane marvel;

and furthermore, because it flashes forth in all states, I greet that speech which speaks through the effort of its own arising, and I bring it face-to-face in order to envelop myself within that state which culminates in the self-reflection of one's true nature.

"What kind [of boat]?"—it refers to that which is like a boat for the thorough crossing of the ocean of doubt; this is to be applied to both [the preceding and following phrases]. This "ocean" is the vast expanse of that very doubt, which is unfathomable and difficult to cross, consisting of the absence of certainty regarding the fullness of the sense of self (*ahaṃtā*), and being a manifold stain of apprehension (*śaṅkā*).

Likewise, it refers to that supreme [state] in which the words (*padāni*)—meaning "resting places"—possess various meanings (*vicitrārthāni*) and serve the purpose of manifold aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*).
In that speech, there are various meaningful words consisting of beautiful compositions and expressive terminology; [the author speaks] of that which is the speech of a guru.

By uttering his own name, whose power is well-known, the author of the treatise inspires those seeking [instruction] with a sense of confidence and demonstrates the great fruitfulness of this treatise through its worthiness of being concealed.

Even though this wealth of knowledge—which is difficult to obtain—is hidden within the cave of the heart, once it is attained, it leads to the welfare of all the world forever, just as it did for Vasugupta.

(VSpk 4.2) *This "wealth" refers to the very knowledge taught in this treatise; because it is the cause for attaining the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*), it is "difficult to obtain," meaning hard to acquire even when not yet possessed.*

Furthermore, having obtained the essence of the instruction from Śaṅkara’s dream, and having acquired from the surface of the stone that very heart which consists of light (*prakāśa*) and awareness (*vimarśa*), he— meaning the master named the venerable Vasugupta— deposited it with certainty (*anta*) within that "cave" (*guhā*), because it provides the space for entry into the interior of the universe; [he deposited] that very wealth of knowledge, just as [described].

That [knowledge] becomes auspicious; likewise, because there is no restriction of authority or limitation, it leads to eternal auspiciousness—that is, to the attainment of immersion in one’s own essential nature which consists of eternal Śiva—for one who diligently conceals within the cave of the heart of all people that which has been placed there, even when not in a formal initiation, and who makes it one's own through firm realization. May there be auspiciousness! VSpkC_4.2:1

"Even though there is no counting of commentaries on this scripture, and although people in this world for the most part possess an upward-turned disposition, those who are wise will understand even the distinction of what we have said; some are like royal swans of consciousness, skilled in extracting the essence. (VSpkC 4.2) [This was written] by one who could not tolerate remaining among the midst of the infinite other commentators.
The Spanda-śāstra has been fully explained by our Guru, but neither he nor I have previously shown even a slight portion of its specific details in the Saṃdoha; however,
today [I shall do so] for one who possesses immersion into the power of Rudra and whose nature is Śiva.
At the intense request of his own disciple named Śūra,
this [work] was determined by Kṣemarāja from the vast [teachings] of his own Guru, the Great Teacher.

For those whose intellect has been clarified by the instructions of true teachers, and for whom the delusion regarding the secret essence (*upaniṣad*) of the illustrious Śiva-teaching has not been shattered;

Those of mild intellect who have never before tasted the nectar of the *Pratyabhijñā* are here authorized by others; let this [work], moreover, be savored by those of full intent. Victorious is that Supreme One, the vibration of consciousness (*saṃvitspanda*), the abode of shimmering, incomparable bliss, whose expansion is this entire universe—from Śiva down to the earth—vastly extended, with a body variegated by the states of manifestation, maintenance, and dissolution of diverse creations. This much is the universe, yet He is but a minute particle of His own unfolding.
